structures.name: Nasal cavity
structures.what: The paired airway from the nostril (via the vestibule) to the [[s.choana]], divided by the [[s.nasal-septum]]; its lateral wall carries the turbinates and meati.
structures.why: Every endonasal operation is done through it, so its width (septum, turbinates) sets your corridor. Know its walls: roof = [[s.cribriform-plate]], floor = hard palate, lateral = turbinates and meati, medial = septum.
structures.ct: Coronal: air space either side of the septum above the hard palate; axial: from nares to the choanae at the posterior edge of the hard palate.
structures.endo: 0°, from the vestibule: septum medially, inferior turbinate head inferolaterally, middle turbinate head superolaterally.

pearls.text: Keep the endoscope on the floor and parallel to the palate first; the nasal cavity is taller than it is wide, and the skull base is only as far away as the scope angle up.
The olfactory cleft (roof) is the narrowest segment; a sponge or packing there risks olfaction and CSF leak after skull base work.

structures.name: Nasal vestibule
structures.what: Skin-lined entrance of the nose inside the nostril, bearing vibrissae, ending at the limen nasi where it meets respiratory mucosa.
structures.why: The scope enters here and every instrument is levered on it; rough entry abrades it and fogs the lens. The nasal sill is the zero point for most intranasal distances.
structures.endo: Seen only on entry; a speculum or the scope sheath retracts the ala laterally.

structures.name: Internal nasal valve
structures.what: The narrowest cross-section of the nasal airway, bounded by the caudal edge of the upper lateral cartilage, the septum, the head of the [[s.inferior-turbinate]] and the floor.
structures.why: It dominates nasal airway resistance, so a septal deviation or turbinate head here obstructs far more than the same deviation further back. Septoplasty and turbinate reduction aim at this area.

rel.note: the valve area includes the IT head

structures.endo: 0°, just inside the vestibule: angle between septum and upper lateral cartilage; the Cottle manoeuvre tests it clinically.

pearls.text: Anterior septal deviations (Mladina types 1–2) act at the valve; posterior deviations matter mainly for surgical access.

structures.name: Nasal floor
structures.what: The floor of the nasal cavity: palatine process of the maxilla anteriorly and horizontal plate of the [[s.palatine-bone]] posteriorly, i.e. the upper surface of the hard palate.
structures.why: The safest route through the nose: along it the scope reaches the [[s.nasopharynx]] with no skull base in front of it. It is also the inferior margin of a medial maxillectomy and a nasoseptal flap incision.

rel.note: the canal descends in the posterior lateral nasal wall, lateral to the floor, to open on the oral surface of the palate

structures.ct: Coronal: the horizontal bone plate of the hard palate; sagittal: from the anterior nasal spine to the posterior nasal spine.
structures.endo: 0°, first pass: follow the floor medial to the IT to the choana.

structures.name: Inferior meatus
structures.what: The space under and lateral to the [[s.inferior-turbinate]]; the [[s.nasolacrimal-duct]] opens into its anterior roof.
structures.why: Home of the valve of Hasner: inferior meatal antrostomy or IT out-fracture must stay posterior to it. It is also the lower limit of a medial maxillectomy.

rel.note: the meatus is the space under the turbinate and against the lateral wall; labeled CT atlases mark its lateral part, beside the turbinate attachment

structures.ct: Coronal: air cleft under the IT, lateral to its free edge; the nasolacrimal canal descends into its roof anteriorly.
structures.endo: 30° or 45°, right or left, with the IT gently medialised: Hasner valve high on the lateral wall about 1 cm behind the IT head.

structures.name: Nasal septum
structures.what: Midline partition of the nasal cavity: [[s.septal-cartilage]] anteriorly, [[s.perpendicular-plate]] of the ethmoid posterosuperiorly, [[s.vomer]] posteroinferiorly, on the [[s.maxillary-crest]].
structures.why: Deviation narrows the corridor and the airway; its mucoperiosteum is the vascularised donor for the [[s.posterior-septal-artery|nasoseptal flap]]. Superiorly it fuses with the cribriform plate, so twisting it can fracture the skull base.

rel.note: perpendicular plate fused to the skull base
vomer alae and perpendicular plate meet the sphenoid rostrum

structures.ct: Coronal and axial: midline bone and cartilage; note spurs, deviation, pneumatisation and the vomer on the rostrum.
structures.endo: 0°, medial to every pass; Kiesselbach area anteroinferiorly, septal swell body opposite the MT head.

pearls.text: Before any endoscopic case, decide whether the septum allows the scope and one instrument to the target; if not, septoplasty first.
For skull base surgery the posterior septectomy (1–2 cm) is what gives binostril four-hand access; decide on a nasoseptal flap before you take it.

At the bony–cartilaginous junction the perichondrium does not run on into the periosteum; dense crossing fibres bind the two layers. Divide them sharply to pass from the subperichondrial onto the subperiosteal plane, or the flap tears here.

structures.name: Septal (quadrangular) cartilage
structures.what: Hyaline cartilage forming the anterior septum; it sits in the groove of the [[s.maxillary-crest]] and between the [[s.perpendicular-plate]] and [[s.vomer]] posteriorly.
structures.why: It carries the dorsal and caudal support of the nose (the [[s.septal-l-strut]]); it is resected or reshaped in septoplasty and is the graft donor site.
structures.ct: Soft tissue density on CT; deviation is inferred from the mucosal outline.
structures.endo: 0°: anterior septum; its caudal border is felt at the columella (hemitransfixion or Killian incision).

pearls.text: Cartilage is avascular: it lives on its perichondrium, so bilateral flap tears opposite each other produce a perforation.

structures.name: Septal L-strut
structures.what: The dorsal and caudal margins of the septal cartilage left intact after septoplasty to support the nasal dorsum and tip; they meet at the anterior septal angle.
structures.why: Resecting or fracturing it causes saddle nose, tip ptosis and columellar retraction. The dorsal limb joins the nasal bones and perpendicular plate at the keystone area, which must never be disarticulated.

pearls.text: Leave at least 10 mm dorsally and caudally ([[m.l-strut-width]]) — several authors set 15 mm as the minimum — and more if the cartilage is thin or already weakened by trauma or prior surgery.

structures.name: Perpendicular plate of the ethmoid
structures.what: Thin midline plate hanging from the [[s.cribriform-plate]], forming the posterosuperior bony septum.
structures.why: It is continuous with the skull base: twisting or rocking it (instead of cutting it) can fracture the cribriform plate and cause a CSF leak. Resect it with through-cutting instruments.
structures.ct: Coronal: midline bony plate continuous with the crista galli above the cribriform plate.
structures.endo: Exposed after elevation of the mucoperichondrium posterior to the bony-cartilaginous junction.

structures.name: Vomer
structures.what: Midline bone forming the posteroinferior septum; its free posterior edge divides the two [[s.choana|choanae]] and its alae clasp the sphenoid rostrum.
structures.why: Its posterior edge is the medial border of the choana, a fixed landmark in the first endoscopic pass. It is removed with the rostrum to create a wide sphenoidotomy or transclival corridor.
structures.ct: Axial and coronal: midline bone on the palate posteriorly; sagittal: runs up and back to the sphenoid rostrum.
structures.endo: 0°, at the choana: the vertical posterior free edge of the septum.

structures.name: Maxillary (nasal) crest
syn: nasal crest of maxilla and palatine
structures.what: The midline ridge formed by the paired maxillae and palatine bones on the nasal floor, on which the septal cartilage and vomer sit; the anterior nasal spine is its front end.
structures.why: Inferior septal spurs and caudal septal dislocation arise here; the cartilage must be freed from it (inferior tunnel) to swing the septum back to the midline.
structures.ct: Coronal: bony midline ridge on the palate, often deviated with a spur (Mladina type 5/6).

pearls.text: Raise the inferior tunnel from the floor (below the spur) and join it to the anterior tunnel: mucosa over a spur is thin and tears if elevated from the spur down.

structures.name: Septal swell body
structures.what: A thickening of erectile, venous-sinusoidal septal mucosa on the upper septum above the inferior turbinate, roughly opposite the middle turbinate head.
structures.why: It can narrow the upper airway and the MT corridor and swells with the nasal cycle; it is reduced with submucosal coblation or radiofrequency when symptomatic, not resected.
structures.ct: Coronal: fusiform soft-tissue thickening of the upper septum at the level of the MT head, above the anterior IT.
structures.endo: 0°: bulge on the septum facing the MT head; decongests markedly.

structures.name: Kiesselbach area
structures.what: Anterior-inferior septal area where septal branches of the [[s.sphenopalatine-artery]], [[s.anterior-ethmoidal-artery]], [[s.greater-palatine-artery]] and superior labial artery anastomose.
structures.why: Source of most (anterior) epistaxis; treat with pressure, topical vasoconstrictor and targeted cautery, not blind packing. Cauterise one side at a time to avoid perforation.
structures.endo: 0° or headlight and speculum: the anterior septum just inside the vestibule.

structures.name: Nasopalatine nerve
structures.what: Branch of [[s.maxillary-nerve|V2]] via the [[s.pterygopalatine-ganglion]] that enters through the [[s.sphenopalatine-foramen]], crosses the sphenoid face and runs down and forward on the septum to the incisive canal.
structures.why: It travels with the posterior septal artery in the nasoseptal flap pedicle and is divided at the incisive canal during flap harvest, leaving anterior palatal numbness (usually temporary).

structures.name: Inferior turbinate
structures.what: Separate scroll-shaped bone covered by thick erectile mucosa, hinged on the lateral nasal wall; the [[s.inferior-meatus]] lies beneath it.
structures.why: It dominates airflow and humidification at the valve; hypertrophy is treated by submucosal reduction that preserves the mucosa. Its ethmoidal process anchors the lower end of the [[s.uncinate-process]].

rel.note: attached to the medial maxillary wall below the natural ostium

structures.ct: Coronal: the lowest and largest turbinate; bone scroll with thick mucosa. Separate soft-tissue from bone hypertrophy before reduction.
structures.endo: 0°: head just behind the valve on the lateral wall; posterior end (tail) near the choana.

pearls.text: Out-fracture (lateralisation) plus submucosal reduction beats resection; never strip the medial mucosa.
Posterior end bleeding after reduction comes from the inferior turbinate branch of the posterior lateral nasal artery ([[s.posterior-lateral-nasal-artery]]).

Its submucosa is erectile: capacitance venous sinusoids fill and empty with sympathetic tone and with the temperature and humidity of inspired air, changing both its bulk and its surface area. That is why it shrinks with decongestant — the basis of the decongestion test before reduction.

structures.name: Middle turbinate
structures.what: Ethmoid turbinate hanging medial to the [[s.middle-meatus]]; anterior part attaches vertically to the skull base (lateral edge of the cribriform plate), middle part turns laterally as the [[s.basal-lamella]] to the [[s.lamina-papyracea]], posterior end attaches to the lateral wall near the [[s.crista-ethmoidalis]].
structures.why: The central landmark of sinus surgery: lateral to it is safe sinus, medial to it (above) is the olfactory cleft and cribriform plate. Its vertical attachment is fragile, and a destabilised MT lateralises and scars the middle meatus shut.

rel.note: posterior attachment points to the SPF
the SPF lies just behind the MT's posterior attachment

structures.ct: Coronal: anterior vertical lamella rising to the skull base at the lateral lamella; check pneumatisation ([[v.concha-bullosa]]) and curvature ([[v.paradoxical-middle-turbinate]]).
structures.endo: 0°: head (anterior end) and axilla on the lateral wall, free edge medial to the uncinate; posterior end at the level of the SPF.

pearls.text: Never grasp and twist the MT; cut, do not pull. Medialise gently with a Freer, never fracture its skull base attachment.
Its axilla (anterior attachment to the lateral wall) is the landmark for the lacrimal sac and the agger nasi cell.
Posterior attachment and horizontal basal lamella are cut in a transpterygoid or posterior ethmoid-to-SPF approach; the SPA lies just behind it.

Partial MT resection is debated: it widens ethmoid access and may reduce lateral scarring and polyp recurrence (lower recurrence at 3 years in one report), but it removes the main landmark for revision. Preserve it during antrostomy when you can; if some must go, take no more than needed, typically the anteroinferior part — the lower half is the usual safe limit, while higher resection risks the cribriform plate — and cauterise the posterior stump, which carries SPA branches.

Its anterior attachment is a reliable guide both to the frontal sinus and to the olfactory fossa, which lies above and medial to the vertical attachment ([[s.olfactory-fossa]]). The most anterior segment often inserts on the frontal sinus floor in front of the cribriform plate, which is why it can be resected in a Draf IIb/III as long as the dissection stays in front of the first olfactory fibre ([[lm.first-olfactory-fiber]]).

structures.name: Superior turbinate
structures.what: Small ethmoid turbinate in the posterior nasal cavity above and behind the middle turbinate; the [[s.superior-meatus]] (posterior ethmoid drainage) lies under it.
structures.why: Its inferior third, when resected, exposes the [[s.sphenoid-ostium]], which lies medial to it in the [[s.sphenoethmoidal-recess]]. It carries olfactory epithelium, so remove only its inferior part — usually the lower third; some surgeons take up to the lower half, never more ([[p.sphenoidotomy]]).

rel.note: sphenoid ostium medial to its inferior edge

structures.ct: Coronal (posterior slices): thin turbinate above the MT tail; sagittal shows the SER medial to it.
structures.endo: 0°, second pass (medial to the MT): the thin lamella at the SER; sphenoid ostium medial to it, about 1–1.5 cm above the choana.

structures.name: Supreme turbinate
structures.what: Inconstant small fourth turbinate above the superior turbinate, with its own supreme meatus draining a posterior ethmoid cell.
structures.why: When present it can be mistaken for the superior turbinate, placing the expected sphenoid ostium too high; count the turbinates from below. The sphenoid ostium relates to the lowest (superior) turbinate.
structures.endo: 0°, SER: a further lamella above the ST; often only on sagittal CT.

structures.name: Lateral nasal wall
structures.what: The lateral boundary of the nasal cavity: turbinates, meati and the medial walls of the maxillary sinus, ethmoid and lacrimal system; built from maxilla, lacrimal, ethmoid, palatine and inferior turbinate bones.
structures.why: All sinus drainage and the whole OMC are on it; its thin areas (fontanelles, lamina papyracea above) decide where you can safely open. The medial maxillectomy removes it.

structures.name: Middle meatus
structures.what: The space lateral to and under the [[s.middle-turbinate]], containing the uncinate, hiatus semilunaris, ethmoidal bulla and the openings of the maxillary, anterior ethmoid and frontal sinuses.
structures.why: The working room for FESS; everything upstream of the OMC is reached through it. Keeping it open post-op (preventing MT lateralisation) is what keeps the sinuses draining.
structures.ct: Coronal: air space between the MT and the lateral wall, above the IT.
structures.endo: 0° or 30°, third pass: under the MT from anterior; uncinate first, bulla behind it.

structures.name: Ostiomeatal complex
structures.what: Functional unit, not a single structure: the [[s.maxillary-natural-ostium]], [[s.ethmoid-infundibulum]], [[s.hiatus-semilunaris]], anterior ethmoid cells, frontal recess and the [[s.middle-meatus]] into which they drain.
structures.why: Narrow clefts where mucosa meets mucosa block mucociliary clearance of the dependent sinuses; Messerklinger and Stammberger showed that opening this bottleneck lets the larger sinuses recover. It is the target of limited FESS.
structures.ct: Coronal CT through the maxillary ostium is the classic OMC view; opacified infundibulum with opacified maxillary sinus = OMC obstruction pattern.

structures.name: Uncinate process
structures.what: Thin sickle-shaped ethmoid lamella on the lateral nasal wall in the middle meatus; it forms the medial wall of the [[s.ethmoid-infundibulum]], its posterior free edge bounds the [[s.hiatus-semilunaris]], and its lower limb attaches to the [[s.inferior-turbinate]].
structures.why: It hides the maxillary natural ostium, so removing it is the first step of almost every FESS. Its superior attachment ([[c.uncinate-superior-attachment]]) decides whether the frontal sinus drains into the infundibulum or the middle meatus.
structures.ct: Coronal: thin bone sloping up from the IT attachment, medial to the infundibulum; axial: sickle anterior to the bulla. Trace its top to classify the superior attachment.
structures.endo: Right or left, 0°, from the middle meatus: crescentic ridge just behind the maxillary line, anterior to the bulla; ball-probe palpation behind it confirms a mobile free edge.

pearls.text: Check on CT that the uncinate is not lateralised onto the orbit (atelectasis, hypoplastic sinus): then the lamina papyracea is immediately behind it.

Take the horizontal (lower) part with a back-biter down to the IT and the upper part with a 45° through-cutter; leave no uncinate remnant, which is the commonest cause of failure to find the natural ostium.

A swing-door uncinectomy (ball probe behind the free edge, uncinate fractured forward and medially) or a retrograde back-biter uncinectomy avoids a sickle knife aimed at the orbit ([[s.lamina-papyracea]]).

structures.name: Ethmoidal infundibulum
structures.what: Three-dimensional cleft between the [[s.uncinate-process]] (medial) and the [[s.lamina-papyracea]] (lateral), opening medially through the [[s.hiatus-semilunaris]]; the maxillary natural ostium lies in its floor.
structures.why: The first bottleneck for maxillary drainage; mucosal disease here obstructs the maxillary sinus. Its lateral wall is the orbit.

rel.note: a cleft off the lateral middle meatus, hidden behind the uncinate

structures.ct: Coronal: air (or opacified) cleft lateral to the uncinate, over the maxillary ostium.
structures.endo: Seen only after uncinectomy; 30°/45°, looking laterally.

structures.name: Hiatus semilunaris (inferior)
structures.what: Two-dimensional crescentic gap between the free posterior edge of the [[s.uncinate-process]] and the anterior face of the [[s.ethmoid-bulla]], connecting the infundibulum to the middle meatus.
structures.why: The ball probe enters here to find the plane behind the uncinate. The superior hiatus (between bulla and MT/basal lamella) leads to the retrobullar recess.
structures.endo: Right or left, 0°/30°, middle meatus: dark crescent between the uncinate edge and the bulla.

structures.name: Recessus terminalis
structures.what: The blind upper end of the [[s.ethmoid-infundibulum]] when the uncinate inserts on the lamina papyracea.
structures.why: When present, the frontal sinus drains medial to the uncinate into the middle meatus; frontal disease is then usually not caused by infundibular disease. Do not mistake it for the frontal ostium.

structures.name: Maxillary line
structures.what: Curvilinear ridge on the lateral nasal wall from the MT axilla down to the IT root, marking the junction of the frontal process of the maxilla with the uncinate process.
structures.why: It marks the anterior attachment of the uncinate, which lies just behind it. It is not the front edge of the lacrimal system: the lacrimal sac lies deep to it (it overlies the lacrimomaxillary suture, about halfway between the lacrimal crests) and the nasolacrimal duct runs deep to it or a few millimetres behind it. DCR mucosal incisions and the anterior limit of uncinectomy and antrostomy are planned from it.
structures.endo: Right or left, 0°: vertical curved ridge in front of the uncinate, from the MT axilla to the IT; palpable with a Freer.

structures.name: Anterior fontanelle
structures.what: Membranous (bone-free) area of the medial maxillary wall below the uncinate, in front of the ethmoidal process of the inferior turbinate.
structures.why: A site of accessory maxillary ostia and a weak spot where instruments enter the sinus unintentionally.

structures.name: Posterior fontanelle
structures.what: Membranous area of the medial maxillary wall behind the uncinate and above the inferior turbinate; the commonest site of an [[v.accessory-maxillary-ostium]].
structures.why: An antrostomy started here is safe (no NLD, no orbit) but must be joined forward to the natural ostium, or mucus recirculates.
structures.endo: Right or left, 0°/30°: soft, depressible area of the lateral wall behind the uncinate; palpate with a probe.

structures.name: Frontal process of the maxilla
structures.what: Thick upward process of the maxilla forming the anterior lacrimal crest and the anterior half of the lacrimal fossa, in front of the maxillary line.
structures.why: The bone removed with a drill or Kerrison in endoscopic DCR to expose the upper lacrimal sac; also removed in an extended prelacrimal or Draf III approach.

rel.note: anterior wall of the lacrimal fossa
the bone taken in front of the sac and duct in DCR and prelacrimal approaches

structures.ct: Axial: thick bone anteromedial to the lacrimal sac; its thickness predicts the drilling needed for DCR.

structures.name: Lacrimal bone
structures.what: Thin, small bone forming the posterior lacrimal fossa (posterior lacrimal crest) between the frontal process of the maxilla and the [[s.lamina-papyracea]].
structures.why: Soft and easily flaked off the posterior sac in DCR; posterior to it is the orbit, so stay on the sac. The uncinate attaches to it.

rel.note: posterior wall of the lacrimal fossa

structures.name: Maxillary sinus
structures.what: The largest paranasal sinus, a pyramid in the body of the maxilla: roof = [[s.orbital-floor]], medial wall = lateral nasal wall, floor = alveolar process, anterior (facial) and posterior (infratemporal) walls; drains through the [[s.maxillary-natural-ostium]].
structures.why: Its ostium sits high on the medial wall, so drainage depends on mucociliary clearance, not gravity. Its walls border the orbit, teeth, PPF and ITF, which is why it is also a corridor.

rel.note: the duct runs in the anteromedial wall of the sinus

structures.ct: Coronal and axial: large air space in the maxilla; check the ostium, infundibulum, infraorbital canal, septa, Haller cells and dental roots.
structures.endo: After antrostomy: 30°/45° for the posterior and medial walls, 70° for the anterior wall, alveolar and zygomatic recesses.

pearls.text: Mucus is carried to the natural ostium even when a larger accessory or surgical opening exists ([[pr.natural-ostium-clearance]]).
Odontogenic sinusitis (unilateral, foul, dental work): treat the tooth as well as the ostium.
Its posterior wall is the gateway to the PPF and ITF: a wide antrostomy plus posterior wall removal exposes IMAX, V2 and the vidian nerve.

structures.name: Maxillary natural ostium
structures.what: The true opening of the maxillary sinus, in the floor of the [[s.ethmoid-infundibulum]], oriented obliquely and hidden behind the [[s.uncinate-process]].
structures.why: Mucociliary clearance converges on it, so every antrostomy must include it. It usually cannot be seen with a 0° scope until the uncinate is removed.
structures.ct: Coronal: the gap in the upper medial maxillary wall leading into the infundibulum, usually at the level of the inferior bulla.
structures.endo: Right or left, 30°/45° after uncinectomy: oval opening in the lower infundibulum, often just above the IT attachment at the level of the bulla; the ball probe slips in and down.

pearls.text: Before the uncinate is removed, expect the ostium at about the junction of the lower third and upper two-thirds of the maxillary line — roughly level with the lower third of the MT.

structures.name: Anterior (facial) wall of maxillary sinus
structures.what: Facial surface of the maxilla from the infraorbital rim to the alveolus, containing the [[s.infraorbital-foramen]] and [[s.canine-fossa]].
structures.why: The hardest wall to reach endoscopically (needs 70° and curved instruments, a canine fossa trephine or a prelacrimal approach). The anterior superior alveolar nerve runs in it.

structures.name: Posterior (infratemporal) wall of maxillary sinus
structures.what: Posterior wall of the antrum, facing the [[s.pterygopalatine-fossa]] medially and the [[s.infratemporal-fossa]] laterally; posterior superior alveolar vessels and nerves run on and in it.
structures.why: Removing it (after a wide antrostomy) is the transmaxillary route to the PPF and ITF. Its periosteum is the plane that protects the IMAX and fat behind it.
structures.ct: Axial: posterior curve of the antrum; the PPF is the fat-filled cleft behind its medial part.

structures.name: Retroantral fat pad
structures.what: Fat behind and lateral to the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus in the anterior infratemporal fossa, continuous laterally with the buccal fat pad and medially with the fat of the [[s.pterygopalatine-fossa]].
structures.why: It is the plane a transmaxillary or medial maxillectomy dissection opens into once the posterior maxillary wall is removed; on CT, an intact, well-defined fat stripe here argues against extension of disease through the wall, while effacement or replacement of the fat by soft-tissue density is a sign that tumour or aggressive sinonasal disease has spread from the antrum into the PPF.
structures.ct: Axial: a clean low-density fat plane behind the posterior maxillary wall on both sides — compare sides. Stranding, effacement or soft-tissue replacement means disease has crossed the posterior wall: an early sign of [[dz.acute-invasive-fungal-sinusitis]] (it can precede visible bone erosion) and of malignant or JNA spread into the infratemporal fossa.

structures.name: Medial wall of maxillary sinus
structures.what: The antral side of the lateral nasal wall: uncinate, fontanelles, IT attachment and inferior meatus, with the nasolacrimal canal in its anterior part.
structures.why: Removed in a medial maxillectomy; the NLD is its anterior limit unless deliberately transected, and the palatine bone and SPF lie at its posterior end.

structures.name: Maxillary sinus floor
structures.what: Floor of the antrum formed by the alveolar process of the maxilla, usually below the nasal floor in adults and related to the roots of the premolars and molars.
structures.why: Dental roots may project into it (odontogenic sinusitis, oroantral fistula after extraction or sublabial surgery). Inferior meatal antrostomies failed mainly because mucociliary clearance still carries mucus to the natural ostium ([[pr.natural-ostium-clearance]]); in adults the floor also lies below the nasal floor, so such a window was not even dependent.

structures.name: Alveolar recess
structures.what: Inferior extension of the maxillary sinus into the alveolar process around the tooth roots.
structures.why: Fungal balls, polyps and inverted papilloma attachments hide here; reaching it endoscopically needs a 70° scope with curved instruments, a medial maxillectomy or a canine fossa port.

structures.name: Zygomatic recess
structures.what: Lateral extension of the maxillary sinus into the zygomatic process.
structures.why: The furthest point from a middle meatal antrostomy; disease here often needs a prelacrimal or canine fossa route.

structures.name: Prelacrimal recess
structures.what: Anteromedial part of the maxillary sinus in front of the nasolacrimal canal, between it and the anterior maxillary wall.
structures.why: Its width ([[c.prelacrimal-recess]]) decides whether the [[p.prelacrimal-approach]] can reach the anterior and lateral antrum without displacing or cutting the NLD.
structures.ct: Axial at the IT level: measure from the anterior maxillary wall to the anterior edge of the nasolacrimal canal.

structures.name: Canine fossa
structures.what: Depression on the anterior maxillary wall below the infraorbital foramen and lateral to the canine eminence; the thinnest part of the anterior wall.
structures.why: Entry point for canine fossa trephination and the Caldwell-Luc antrostomy; placed too medially or high it injures the anterior superior alveolar nerve or the infraorbital nerve.

structures.name: Infraorbital nerve
structures.what: Terminal continuation of [[s.maxillary-nerve|V2]] after it enters the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure; runs in the infraorbital groove and canal of the orbital floor and exits at the [[s.infraorbital-foramen]] to supply the cheek, lower lid, side of nose and upper lip.
structures.why: Visible as a ridge on the antral roof, sometimes dehiscent or hanging on a bony septum ([[c.infraorbital-canal]]); debriding or drilling on it causes cheek numbness and dysaesthesia. Followed backwards, it leads to V2 and foramen rotundum.

rel.note: follow it back through the PPF

structures.ct: Coronal: canal or groove in the orbital floor; note if it protrudes into the antrum on a septum (type 3).
structures.endo: 45°/70° after wide antrostomy: ridge running anteroposteriorly across the antral roof.

structures.name: Infraorbital canal
structures.what: Groove then canal in the orbital floor carrying the infraorbital nerve and vessels from the inferior orbital fissure to the infraorbital foramen.
structures.why: Its relation to the antral roof (embedded, bulging or suspended on a septum) predicts nerve injury with angled instruments.

structures.name: Infraorbital foramen
structures.what: Opening on the anterior maxillary wall below the inferior orbital rim where the infraorbital nerve emerges onto the face.
structures.why: The superior limit of any anterior maxillary wall window; canine fossa punctures are placed well below and lateral to the canine root, away from it.

rel.note: an anterior maxillary window lies between the duct medially and the nerve above and laterally

structures.name: Anterior superior alveolar nerve
structures.what: Branch of the infraorbital nerve given off in the canal that runs down in the anterior maxillary wall to the incisors and canine.
structures.why: Injured by canine fossa puncture, Caldwell-Luc and anterior extension of a prelacrimal approach: dental and upper-lip numbness or dysaesthesia.

structures.name: Posterior superior alveolar artery
structures.what: Branch of the IMAX in the PPF/ITF that runs down on the posterior maxillary wall (maxillary tuberosity) with the posterior superior alveolar nerves.
structures.why: A troublesome bleeder when the posterior maxillary wall is removed laterally in transmaxillary PPF/ITF exposure; coagulate before cutting.

structures.name: Lacrimal sac
structures.what: Membranous sac in the lacrimal fossa of the medial orbital wall, receiving the canaliculi and continuing down as the [[s.nasolacrimal-duct]].
structures.why: The target of DCR; its fundus lies well above the MT axilla, so a DCR that opens only its lower part fails. Posterior to it is the orbit.
structures.ct: Axial: soft tissue in the lacrimal fossa between the anterior and posterior lacrimal crests; CT dacryocystography outlines it.
structures.endo: Right or left, 0°: deep to the frontal process of the maxilla (anterior half) and the lacrimal bone (posterior half), centred under the maxillary line and extending well above the MT axilla; light-pipe transillumination through the canaliculus confirms it.

pearls.text: The sac extends about 8–10 mm above the axilla ([[m.lacrimal-sac-above-axilla]]); expose it fully and marsupialise it so the common canaliculus opening lies in the open ostium.

structures.name: Lacrimal canaliculi and common canaliculus
structures.what: Upper and lower canaliculi run from the puncta medially and usually unite as a common canaliculus entering the lateral wall of the lacrimal sac (internal common punctum).
structures.why: Probes and stents pass through them; forceful probing creates false passages. Canalicular obstruction is not fixed by a DCR.

structures.name: Lacrimal fossa
structures.what: Bony groove on the medial orbital wall formed by the frontal process of the maxilla (anterior lacrimal crest) and the lacrimal bone (posterior lacrimal crest), holding the lacrimal sac.
structures.why: The bone removed in DCR: thick maxillary part anteriorly (drill or Kerrison), thin lacrimal part posteriorly (flake with a round knife).

structures.name: Nasolacrimal duct
structures.what: Duct from the lacrimal sac down through the bony nasolacrimal canal, in the anterior medial maxillary wall, to open under the IT in the [[s.inferior-meatus]] at the valve of Hasner.
structures.why: It lies just anterior to the maxillary natural ostium, so an antrostomy extended forwards cuts it (epiphora). It is the anterior limit of a medial maxillectomy unless deliberately divided.
structures.ct: Axial: round lucent canal in the anteromedial maxilla; coronal: descending from the orbit to under the IT.
structures.endo: Not normally visible; its bony canal lies deep to the maxillary line and the anterior attachment of the uncinate, so hard bone at the anterior antrostomy margin is the canal. Hasner valve is seen with a 30°/45° in the inferior meatus.

pearls.text: When enlarging an antrostomy, go posteriorly and inferiorly; hard bone anteriorly means the NLD canal ([[pr.antrostomy-posterior-inferior]]).
In a medial maxillectomy, divide it sharply and obliquely (not crushed) high in the canal and consider marsupialising it to avoid stenosis.

structures.name: Valve of Hasner
structures.what: Mucosal fold at the lower opening of the nasolacrimal duct in the lateral wall of the inferior meatus, roughly 1 cm behind the IT head.
structures.why: The anterior limit for inferior meatal work; it is the site of congenital NLD obstruction (probed in infants).
structures.endo: 30°/45°, right or left, inferior meatus: slit or pore high on the lateral wall; pressing on the medial canthus may express fluid.

pearls.text: From the front of the nose the valve lies roughly 30–35 mm behind the limen nasi along the inferior meatus (textbook estimate), about 10–15 mm behind the IT head ([[m.hasner-behind-it-head]]); medial maxillectomy and inferior meatal cuts start behind it.

structures.name: Palatine bone
structures.what: L-shaped bone: horizontal plate (posterior hard palate) and perpendicular plate (posterior lateral nasal wall and medial wall of the PPF), topped by orbital and sphenoidal processes that frame the [[s.sphenopalatine-foramen]].
structures.why: Its perpendicular plate is the thin bone removed to enter the PPF medially; its crista ethmoidalis is the SPA landmark; the greater palatine canal runs between it and the maxilla.

structures.name: Perpendicular plate of the palatine bone
structures.what: Thin vertical plate of the palatine bone behind the maxillary sinus that forms the medial wall of the PPF and carries the crista ethmoidalis.
structures.why: Removed (after the SPA is controlled) to open the PPF from the nose; the descending palatine canal lies in its lateral junction with the maxilla.

structures.name: Crista ethmoidalis
syn: ethmoidal crest of the palatine bone
structures.what: Small bony ridge on the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone, where the posterior end of the MT attaches, immediately anterior to the [[s.sphenopalatine-foramen]].
structures.why: The sentinel for SPA ligation: raise the mucoperiosteal flap back to it, remove it, and the SPA branches lie behind. It is consistently present.
structures.endo: Right or left, 0°/30°, after a posterior middle meatal flap: sharp vertical bony ridge; vessels emerge just behind it.

pearls.text: In cadaver dissections the crista lies within about 1 mm of the SPF in roughly 95% of specimens (textbook-reported figure), so taking it down almost always exposes the foramen.

structures.name: Sphenopalatine foramen
structures.what: Opening between the orbital and sphenoidal processes of the palatine bone and the sphenoid body, connecting the PPF with the nasal cavity near the posterior end of the MT. It usually spans the junction of the middle and superior meati behind the crista ethmoidalis, but opens only into the superior meatus in about a third of sides.
structures.why: Where the SPA and the posterior nasal nerves enter the nose; the key to posterior epistaxis control and the medial door of the PPF.
structures.ct: Axial and coronal: gap in the medial PPF wall behind the MT tail, above the level of its horizontal attachment.
structures.endo: Right or left, 0°/30°: behind the crista ethmoidalis after raising the lateral wall flap; vessels and nerves in a fat-containing opening.

structures.name: Internal maxillary artery
structures.what: Terminal branch of the external carotid artery: 1st (mandibular) part behind the mandibular neck, 2nd (pterygoid) part on the lateral pterygoid muscle in the ITF, 3rd (pterygopalatine) part looping in the anterior PPF and ending as the [[s.sphenopalatine-artery]].
structures.why: Its 3rd part lies in the anterior, vascular layer of the PPF in front of the nerves; it is clipped for refractory posterior epistaxis and must be controlled and mobilised to reach V2, the vidian nerve and the pterygoid base.
structures.ct: CTA/MRA: tortuous loop in the PPF; axial CT shows the fat plane where it lies.
structures.endo: Transmaxillary 0°, after posterior wall and periosteum removal: tortuous artery in fat, in front of the neural plane.

pearls.text: Branches of the 3rd part: posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, descending palatine, artery of the pterygoid canal, pharyngeal (palatovaginal), sphenopalatine.

structures.name: Sphenopalatine artery
structures.what: Terminal branch of the IMAX; enters the nose through the [[s.sphenopalatine-foramen]] and divides into the [[s.posterior-lateral-nasal-artery]] and the [[s.posterior-septal-artery]], often before it exits the foramen.
structures.why: The main supply of the nasal cavity (up to about 90% of its mucosa by textbook estimate) and the source of most posterior epistaxis; ligation must catch every branch, including the posterior septal artery running across the sphenoid face.
structures.endo: Right or left, 0°/30°: behind the crista ethmoidalis after a posterior middle meatal flap; frequently 2 or more trunks.

structures.name: Posterior lateral nasal artery
structures.what: Branch of the SPA supplying the lateral nasal wall: middle and inferior turbinate branches that run into the posterior ends of the turbinates.
structures.why: Bleeds when an antrostomy is taken too far back, at the MT tail during posterior work, and at the IT tail after turbinate reduction.

structures.name: Posterior septal artery
structures.what: Branch of the SPA that crosses the anterior face of the sphenoid between the [[s.sphenoid-ostium]] above and the [[s.choana]] below, then runs forward on the septum.
structures.why: The pedicle of the nasoseptal flap and a cause of brisk bleeding when a sphenoidotomy is extended inferiorly or a posterior septectomy is done. Missing it is a reason SPA ligation fails.
structures.endo: 0°, midline: runs obliquely across the rostrum below the sphenoid ostium; Doppler can confirm the pedicle.

pearls.text: Before sphenoidotomy in any case where skull base reconstruction might be needed, keep the inferior sphenoidotomy margin above the pedicle or raise a rescue flap first.

structures.name: Descending palatine artery
structures.what: Branch of the IMAX 3rd part that descends from the PPF through the greater palatine canal to become the [[s.greater-palatine-artery]].
structures.why: Crosses the field when the medial PPF wall and the posterior maxillary wall are removed; sacrificing it is usually tolerated but causes brisk bleeding if torn.

structures.name: Greater palatine artery
structures.what: Continuation of the descending palatine artery; exits the greater palatine foramen, runs forward on the hard palate and ascends through the incisive canal to the anterior septum.
structures.why: Contributes to the Kiesselbach area. Its foramen is the entry point for a greater palatine canal injection, which infiltrates the PPF to vasoconstrict the IMAX/SPA territory for posterior epistaxis or intraoperative haemostasis.

structures.name: Greater palatine canal and foramen
structures.what: Canal from the floor of the PPF down between maxilla and palatine bone to the greater palatine foramen on the posterolateral hard palate (usually opposite the 2nd–3rd molar), carrying the descending palatine vessels and greater palatine nerve.
structures.why: The route of a transpalatal PPF injection (vasoconstriction, hemostasis) and a landmark for the lower PPF when drilling the posterior maxilla medially.

rel.note: descends behind the posteromedial corner of the sinus, between maxilla and palatine bone

structures.name: Woodruff's area
structures.what: Area on the posterior lateral nasal wall near the posterior end of the IT and inferior meatus, classically described as a venous plexus; arterial supply from posterior lateral nasal branches of the SPA.
structures.why: A classic source of posterior epistaxis in older adults; hard to see without endoscopy. Its venous vs arterial nature is debated.

structures.name: Pterygopalatine fossa
structures.what: Small inverted-pyramid space between the posterior maxilla (anterior), the pterygoid process (posterior) and the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone (medial), opening laterally through the pterygomaxillary fissure into the ITF.
structures.why: A neurovascular crossroads: vascular layer (IMAX) anteriorly, neural layer (V2, PPG, vidian) posteriorly. It connects to orbit, middle fossa, nose, oral cavity, ITF and nasopharynx, which is why tumours (JNA, schwannoma, perineural spread) spread through it.

rel.note: anterolateral; the lateral recess lies behind it across the pterygoid base (transpterygoid route)

structures.ct: Axial: fat-filled cleft behind the maxillary sinus; loss of its fat (or widening) signals tumour. Its foramina (rotundum, vidian, palatovaginal, SPF, greater palatine) are the escape routes to check.

pearls.text: Openings: foramen rotundum and vidian canal (posterior wall, superolateral and inferomedial), palatovaginal canal, SPF (medial), inferior orbital fissure (superior), pterygomaxillary fissure (lateral), greater palatine canal (inferior).

structures.name: Pterygopalatine ganglion
structures.what: Parasympathetic ganglion in the PPF, suspended below V2, receiving the vidian nerve and giving nasal, palatine, pharyngeal and orbital branches (secretomotor to lacrimal and nasal glands).
structures.why: Target of vidian/posterior nasal neurectomy and SPG block; it lies in the posterior, neural layer, behind the IMAX.

structures.name: Maxillary nerve (V2)
structures.what: Second division of the trigeminal nerve: leaves the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, exits the skull through [[s.foramen-rotundum]] into the upper PPF, and continues through the inferior orbital fissure as the [[s.infraorbital-nerve]].
structures.why: In the PPF it is the superolateral landmark (with the vidian canal inferomedially) framing the pterygoid base; the upper transpterygoid corridor to Meckel's cave runs between them. Injury numbs the cheek.
structures.ct: Coronal: foramen rotundum in the sphenoid, superolateral to the vidian canal; may bulge into a pneumatised lateral recess.

structures.name: Foramen rotundum
structures.what: Short canal in the greater sphenoid wing from the middle cranial fossa to the upper posterior PPF, transmitting V2.
structures.why: Superolateral corner of the pterygoid base; drilling between it and the vidian canal enters the lateral recess of the sphenoid and leads to Meckel's cave.

rel.note: on the lateral sphenoid wall the optic prominence is above, V2 below and lateral
opens into the upper posterior wall of the fossa

structures.ct: Coronal: round canal superolateral to the vidian canal on the anterior sphenoid.

structures.name: Vidian nerve
structures.what: Formed at the foramen lacerum by the greater superficial petrosal (parasympathetic) and deep petrosal (sympathetic) nerves; runs forward in the [[s.vidian-canal]] to the PPG.
structures.why: Carries lacrimal and nasal secretomotor fibres (vidian neurectomy for rhinorrhoea costs tear production). Followed backwards it leads to the anterior genu of the petrous ICA at the foramen lacerum.

rel.note: leads to the anterior genu of the petrous ICA

structures.name: Vidian canal
structures.what: Canal in the base of the pterygoid process at the junction with the sphenoid body, running from the foramen lacerum area forwards to the posterior PPF; carries the vidian nerve and artery.
structures.why: The key landmark for the petrous ICA in transpterygoid surgery: drill around its inferomedial circumference and you reach the anterior genu safely. It often forms a ridge in the sphenoid floor.
structures.ct: Coronal: small canal at the pterygoid base below and medial to foramen rotundum; axial: runs anteroposteriorly to the foramen lacerum.
structures.endo: After PPF exposure, 0°: nerve entering the posterior PPF wall inferomedial to V2; in a well-pneumatised sphenoid, a ridge in the floor.

structures.name: Artery of the pterygoid canal
structures.what: Small artery running with the vidian nerve, usually from the IMAX 3rd part; it may anastomose with the petrous ICA.
structures.why: Bleeds when the vidian canal is opened; it is a feeder in juvenile angiofibroma (with ICA supply). Coagulate with bipolar, never pack blindly into the canal toward the ICA.

structures.name: Palatovaginal canal
structures.what: Small canal between the sphenoidal process of the palatine bone and the vaginal process of the sphenoid, medial to the vidian canal, carrying the pharyngeal branch of the IMAX and PPG to the nasopharynx.
structures.why: Confused with the vidian canal; it is smaller and more medial. Its artery bleeds when the sphenoid floor/pterygoid base is drilled.

structures.name: Greater palatine nerve
structures.what: Branch of V2 through the PPG descending in the greater palatine canal to supply the hard palate mucosa.
structures.why: Injured when the lower PPF or posterior maxilla is taken down: palatal numbness.

structures.name: Posterior nasal nerve
structures.what: Nasal branches from the PPG that enter through the SPF (and small accessory foramina) with the SPA, supplying secretomotor and sensory fibres to the turbinates and septum.
structures.why: Target of posterior nasal neurectomy (and cryo/radiofrequency ablation) for rhinorrhoea, avoiding the dry eye of vidian neurectomy.

structures.name: Pterygomaxillary fissure
structures.what: Vertical slit between the posterior maxilla and the lateral pterygoid plate connecting the PPF with the ITF.
structures.why: The IMAX enters the PPF through it and tumours (JNA) leave through it into the ITF; widening on CT is a classic sign.

rel.note: the lateral (ITF) and medial (nasal) doors of the PPF

structures.name: Inferior orbital fissure
structures.what: Fissure between the orbital floor and greater sphenoid wing linking the orbit with the PPF and ITF; V2 becomes the infraorbital nerve here.
structures.why: Route of tumour and infection spread from PPF to orbit; the superior limit of PPF dissection.

rel.note: the two fissures diverge from the orbital apex

structures.name: Pterygoid process
structures.what: Downward process of the sphenoid behind the PPF: a base (containing the vidian canal) and the [[s.medial-pterygoid-plate]] and [[s.lateral-pterygoid-plate]], separated by the pterygoid fossa.
structures.why: Drilling its base (transpterygoid approach) opens the lateral sphenoid recess, Meckel's cave and the petrous ICA; its plates are the gate to the ITF and ET.
structures.ct: Axial and coronal: medial and lateral plates behind the maxillary tuberosity; the base may be pneumatised by the sphenoid.

structures.name: Medial pterygoid plate
structures.what: Thin medial plate of the pterygoid process forming the lateral boundary of the choana, ending in the hamulus; the ET cartilage lies against its upper posterior edge.
structures.why: Landmark for the cartilaginous ET and the lateral limit of the nasopharynx; removed in medial transpterygoid and nasopharyngectomy.

structures.name: Lateral pterygoid plate
structures.what: Broad lateral plate of the pterygoid process; origin of the lateral (outer surface) and medial (inner surface) pterygoid muscles.
structures.why: Following its posterior edge up to the skull base leads to the [[s.foramen-ovale]] and V3, the key ITF landmark.

structures.name: Infratemporal fossa
structures.what: Space below the middle cranial fossa, lateral to the lateral pterygoid plate and medial to the mandibular ramus, containing the pterygoid muscles, IMAX (1st–2nd parts), pterygoid venous plexus, V3 and its branches.
structures.why: Reached endonasally by extending a transmaxillary/transpterygoid corridor laterally (or via a Denker/prelacrimal route); V3 and the parapharyngeal ICA set its posterior limits.
structures.ct: Axial: fat and muscle behind the maxilla lateral to the pterygoid plates; widening of the pterygomaxillary fissure or loss of fat suggests tumour.

structures.name: Lateral pterygoid muscle
structures.what: Two-headed muscle from the greater wing and lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate to the mandibular condyle and TMJ disc; the IMAX 2nd part runs on (or deep to) it.
structures.why: The first muscle met in the ITF after the PPF; bleeding from its venous plexus is brisk. Resection or retraction exposes V3 behind it.

structures.name: Medial pterygoid muscle
structures.what: Muscle from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate (and maxillary tuberosity) to the medial angle of the mandible.
structures.why: Postoperative trismus follows injury to the pterygoid muscles in ITF/transpterygoid surgery.

structures.name: Pterygoid venous plexus
structures.what: Venous network around the lateral pterygoid muscle, connecting to the cavernous sinus (via emissary veins), the facial vein and the maxillary vein.
structures.why: Profuse venous bleeding in the ITF, controlled with head-up position, pressure and haemostatic agents rather than cautery; also a route for infection to the cavernous sinus.

structures.name: Mandibular nerve (V3)
structures.what: Third division of the trigeminal nerve, exiting [[s.foramen-ovale]] into the ITF behind the lateral pterygoid plate; branches include the lingual, inferior alveolar and muscular nerves.
structures.why: The posterolateral limit of endonasal ITF dissection; the parapharyngeal ICA lies posteromedial to V3 and posterolateral to the cartilaginous ET.

structures.name: Foramen ovale
structures.what: Opening in the greater sphenoid wing, posterolateral to the lateral pterygoid plate root, transmitting V3; foramen spinosum (middle meningeal artery) lies posterolateral to it.
structures.why: Reached endonasally by following the posterior edge of the lateral pterygoid plate up to the skull base.

rel.note: posterolateral, at the posterior root of the lateral pterygoid plate

structures.ct: Axial skull base: oval foramen posterolateral to the pterygoid base; foramen spinosum just behind and lateral.

structures.name: Foramen spinosum
structures.what: Small round foramen in the greater sphenoid wing, posterolateral to the foramen ovale, transmitting the middle meningeal artery (and vein) into the middle fossa.
structures.why: It is the constant landmark for the middle meningeal artery and marks the posterolateral limit of dissection along the greater wing in lateral infratemporal-fossa extensions of the transpterygoid corridor.
structures.ct: Axial skull base bone window: small round foramen just posterolateral to the foramen ovale in the greater wing.

structures.name: Middle meningeal artery
structures.what: Branch of the IMAX 1st part in the ITF that ascends through the foramen spinosum to the middle fossa dura.
structures.why: Marks the posterolateral depth of ITF dissection; coagulated in some middle fossa/ITF tumours.

structures.name: Nasopharynx
structures.what: Upper pharynx behind the [[s.choana|choanae]] and above the soft palate; roof under the sphenoid body and basiocciput, lateral walls with the ET orifices, tori and fossae of Rosenmüller, posterior-superior wall with the adenoid.
structures.why: The endpoint of the first endoscopic pass and of all sinus mucociliary clearance; its lateral recess is the commonest origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, so inspect it in every unilateral OME or neck mass.
structures.ct: Axial: air space behind the choanae; asymmetry of the fossa of Rosenmüller or longus colli fat is significant.
structures.endo: 0°, first pass along the floor: through the choana, look laterally to each ET orifice and fossa.

structures.name: Choana
structures.what: Posterior opening of each nasal cavity into the nasopharynx, bounded by the vomer (medial), medial pterygoid plate (lateral), sphenoid body (roof) and horizontal palatine plate (floor).
structures.why: The fixed landmark of the posterior nose: the sphenoid ostium lies about 1–1.5 cm above the choanal arch, and the posterior septal artery crosses the sphenoid face between them.

rel.note: sphenoid ostium ~1–1.5 cm above the arch

structures.endo: 0°, end of the floor pass: arched opening; ET orifice seen laterally beyond it.

structures.name: Eustachian tube (nasopharyngeal end)
structures.what: Tube from the middle ear to the lateral nasopharynx; its cartilaginous medial two-thirds opens behind the IT tail at an orifice framed posterosuperiorly by the [[s.torus-tubarius]].
structures.why: Obstruction by tumour or adenoid gives OME, so a unilateral OME in an adult means inspecting the nasopharynx.

rel.note: parapharyngeal ICA posterolateral to the cartilaginous ET

structures.endo: 0°, from the choana: orifice on the lateral nasopharyngeal wall about 1–1.5 cm behind the IT tail.

pearls.text: The cartilaginous ET is the landmark for the parapharyngeal ICA, which lies posterolateral to it, in nasopharyngectomy and endonasal ITF approaches ([[pr.itf-landmarks]]).

structures.name: Torus tubarius
structures.what: Mucosa-covered prominence of the medial ET cartilage forming the posterosuperior lip of the ET orifice.
structures.why: Injury (adenoidectomy, debrider) scars the orifice; behind it lies the fossa of Rosenmüller.

structures.name: Fossa of Rosenmüller
structures.what: Deep recess of the lateral nasopharyngeal wall behind and above the torus tubarius.
structures.why: The commonest origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma: look into it with a 0° or 30° scope in every unilateral OME. The parapharyngeal/petrous ICA lies deep and lateral to it, so never biopsy deeply or debride blindly.
structures.ct: Axial: symmetric air-filled recess; asymmetry or effacement warrants biopsy.
structures.endo: 0°/30°, from the choana, turn the scope laterally behind the torus.

structures.name: Adenoid (nasopharyngeal tonsil)
structures.what: Lymphoid tissue on the posterosuperior wall of the nasopharynx, large in childhood and regressing in adolescence.
structures.why: Obstructs the choanae and ETs in children; an adult adenoid-like mass warrants biopsy (lymphoma, NPC, HIV).
structures.endo: 0°, from the choana: lobulated tissue on the posterior wall.

structures.name: Tensor veli palatini
structures.what: Muscle from the scaphoid fossa and lateral ET cartilage, hooking round the pterygoid hamulus into the palatine aponeurosis; opens the ET.
structures.why: Lies lateral to the ET cartilage; in endonasal ITF/parapharyngeal dissection it is the plane immediately anterior to the parapharyngeal ICA.

structures.name: Levator veli palatini
structures.what: Muscle from the petrous apex and medial ET cartilage into the soft palate, forming the levator fold beneath the ET orifice.
structures.why: Medial to tensor; a landmark in nasopharyngeal and ET dissection toward the petrous apex.

structures.name: Septal mucosa
structures.what: The lining of each side of the septum: mucoperichondrium over the [[s.septal-cartilage]] and mucoperiosteum over the [[s.perpendicular-plate]] and [[s.vomer]]. It is the tissue the nasoseptal flap is raised from.
structures.why: The flap's blood supply travels in this lining: the [[s.posterior-septal-artery]] and its branches run in it, so it is raised in a subperichondrial and subperiosteal plane, and the donor side then lacks lining until it remucosalizes. A tear in the lining on both sides at the same place leaves the avascular cartilage bare ([[h.septal-perforation]]).
structures.ct: Not separable from the cartilage and bone beneath it on CT; the lining is the air/tissue boundary.

structures.name: Nasal floor and inferior meatus mucosa
structures.what: The mucoperiosteum of the nasal floor, continuing laterally into the [[s.inferior-meatus]]. The extended nasoseptal flap takes it together with the septal mucosa.
structures.why: It adds length and area for large defects: in a cadaver and CT series the extended flap was about 20 mm longer and added about 774 mm² ([[m.nsf-extended-gain]]). The reference specimen has no surface for it yet.

structures.name: Posterior septal artery, superior branch
structures.what: The upper of the two septal branches into which the [[s.posterior-septal-artery]] divides on the sphenoid face or at the back of the septum.
structures.why: Both branches lie inside the nasoseptal flap pedicle. In one latex-injected series the dominant branch always lay below the axial plane of the sphenoid ostium, so the upper rim of the pedicle is set by the ostium.
structures.endo: Not separately visible; Doppler over the pedicle confirms flow, not which branch.

structures.name: Posterior septal artery, inferior branch
structures.what: The lower of the two septal branches of the [[s.posterior-septal-artery]]. It was the dominant branch in about three of five sides in one series, and may run downward before turning anteroinferiorly along the septum.
structures.why: Two high-risk places for the flap design were identified in that series: the inferior aspect of the sphenoid ostium and the junction of the posterior septum with the choanal arch. This branch passes close to both.

structures.name: Nasopalatine artery
structures.what: The artery of the anteroinferior septum that runs to the [[s.incisive-canal]]. In the Kiesselbach area it meets the [[s.greater-palatine-artery]], the septal branch of the superior labial artery and the anterior ethmoidal artery.
structures.why: With the septal branch of the superior labial artery it supplies the bipedicled anterior septal flap, an option for frontal table coverage when the posterior pedicle is not available ([[m.bas-flap-length]]).

structures.name: Incisive canal
structures.what: Canal through the anterior hard palate, behind the central incisors, joining the floor of the nose beside the septum to the mouth. It carries the [[s.nasopalatine-nerve]] and the nasopalatine artery.
structures.why: The anterior limit of the bipedicled anterior septal flap's long axis ([[m.bas-flap-length]]). Its neurovascular bundle can be large enough to cause clinically significant trauma if the canal is entered.
structures.ct: The canal is visible in the reference specimen on the midsagittal plane, running from the nasal floor anteroinferiorly through the anterior maxilla ([[lm.incisive-canal]]).

structures.name: Superior labial artery
structures.what: Branch of the facial artery running in the upper lip. Its septal branch ascends into the anterior septum; its nasal-septal branches also supply the nasal tip.
structures.why: The external end of the anterior septal arterial arcade, and the source of the anterior pedicle of the bipedicled anterior septal flap.

structures.name: Septal branch of the superior labial artery
structures.what: The branch of the [[s.superior-labial-artery]] that enters the anterior septum near the columella and ascends in its lining.
structures.why: One of the arteries joining at the Kiesselbach area, and one of the two pedicles of the bipedicled anterior septal flap.

structures.name: Facial artery
structures.what: External carotid branch crossing the face. It gives off the [[s.superior-labial-artery]] and the lateral nasal branches of the external nose.
structures.why: The external-carotid source for the anteroinferior septum and the external nose, in contrast to the ophthalmic (internal carotid) source of the anterior ethmoidal and dorsal nasal arteries: the two systems anastomose in the nose.

structures.name: External nose
structures.what: The skin, musculoaponeurotic layer, five named cartilages (two lateral, two alar, one septal) and nasal bones that form the nose outside the piriform aperture.
structures.why: It is the fulcrum for every instrument: the nostril sets how far and in which directions a scope can swing. In the reference specimen it was masked away, so the endoscope pivots on a provisional point.

pearls.text: Most of the arteries of the nose run superficial to the musculoaponeurotic layer. The lateral and dorsal nasal arteries and the columellar branches form an alar arcade, so an external approach dissected below that layer preserves the main supply of the tip.

structures.name: Lateral nasal artery
structures.what: Branch of the facial system to the side of the external nose and the alar region. It is not the posterior lateral nasal artery of the sphenopalatine system ([[s.posterior-lateral-nasal-artery]]).
structures.why: The main supply of the nasal tip in most sides of an Asian cadaver series; it forms an alar arcade with the dorsal nasal and columellar arteries.

structures.name: Dorsal nasal artery
structures.what: Ophthalmic-system artery of the nasal dorsum; it joins the lateral nasal branches of the facial system in the superficial layer over the nasal dorsum.
structures.why: The internal carotid contribution to the external nose, and the main tip supply in a minority of sides.

structures.name: Columellar arteries
structures.what: Small arteries rising through the columella to the nasal tip. They are narrow and vary in size and number.
structures.why: They are crossed by a transcolumellar incision, but are a variable and usually minor contribution to the tip, so the tip does not depend on them.

structures.name: External nasal valve
structures.what: The nostril aperture, bounded by the alar rim, the columella and the nasal sill. Its shape is held by the alar cartilages.
structures.why: Collapse here narrows the airway at the entrance, and the aperture is where the scope enters and the fulcrum sits: an alar rim pushed laterally changes how far the shaft can swing.

structures.name: Nasal ala
structures.what: The mobile wing of the external nose forming the lateral wall of the nostril and its rim.
structures.why: The scope sheath retracts it laterally on entry ([[s.nasal-vestibule]]).

structures.name: Columella
structures.what: The soft-tissue strut between the two nostrils; the visible part of the septum, formed by the medial crura of the alar cartilages.
structures.why: The medial wall of the nostril. Transfixion and hemitransfixion incisions are made at its caudal septal border.

structures.name: Nasal bone
structures.what: Small paired bone forming the nasal ridge between the frontal processes of the maxillae. Its free lower edge continues as the lateral (upper lateral) cartilage.
structures.why: The bony roof of the external nose and the upper border of the piriform aperture; the procerus and nasalis muscles attach to its outer surface.

structures.name: Piriform aperture
structures.what: The pear-shaped bony opening of the front of the skull into the nose, bounded by the nasal bones above and the maxillae to the sides and below; the anterior nasal spine projects from its floor.
structures.why: The bony limit of every transnasal movement: the scope's fulcrum lies in front of it, and the rim of the aperture lies behind the nostril.

structures.name: Hard palate
structures.what: The anterior, immobile bony part of the palate, about two-thirds of its surface area: palatine processes of the maxilla in front and horizontal plates of the palatine bones behind. Its upper surface is the floor of the nasal cavity and is lined with respiratory epithelium; its lower surface is the roof of the mouth and is lined with oral mucosa containing salivary glands.
structures.why: It separates the nose from the mouth: the floor of the nose and the roof of the mouth are the two faces of one bony plate, lined by respiratory epithelium above and oral mucosa below. See [[s.nasal-floor]] for its upper surface, [[s.palatine-bone]] for its posterior bone, and [[s.incisive-canal]] and [[s.greater-palatine-canal]] for the passages through it.

structures.name: Parapharyngeal space
structures.what: Fascial space shaped like an inverted pyramid, its base at the skull base and its apex toward the greater cornu of the hyoid bone. It is limited anteriorly by the pterygomandibular raphe, laterally by the inner fascia of the masticatory space and the deep lobe of the parotid gland, medially by the buccopharyngeal and alar fasciae, and, generally, posteriorly by the posterior fascia of the carotid sheath. A fascia running back from the styloid process to the tensor veli palatini divides it into prestyloid (anterior) and poststyloid (posterior) compartments.
structures.why: Tumours of the upper space are reached endonasally by a transpterygoid route, with or without an anterior transmaxillary corridor. The medial pterygoid, tensor veli palatini and levator veli palatini muscles are the key landmarks into the upper space; the lateral pterygoid plate, foramen ovale and mandibular nerve guide the surgeon to the parapharyngeal internal carotid artery. The combined approach also gave a better view of the inferior limit of the upper space and eased control of the ICA.

pearls.text: Where the prestyloid/poststyloid boundary lies is not agreed: a scoping review of 202 studies found the tensor-vascular-styloid fascia named in 43.6% of them and the styloid diaphragm in 30.7%, with several other structures in smaller shares, and proposed that the styloid diaphragm divides the space coronally. Use the term with the dividing structure named.

Endoscopic dissection (six heads): after enlarging the sinonasal corridor and drilling the pterygoid process below the nasal floor, a fat pad of the upper space lay between the tensor veli palatini and the medial pterygoid muscles, forming the lateral space; retracting those muscles exposed the levator veli palatini, and removing the soft tissue between the tensor and the superior constrictor exposed the medial space, which was dissected posteriorly to reach the poststyloid compartment.

structures.name: Prestyloid parapharyngeal compartment
structures.what: The anterior compartment of the parapharyngeal space, in front of the fascia that runs back from the styloid process to the tensor veli palatini. The endonasal dissection finds fat in it.
structures.why: Reached endonasally once the lateral pterygoid plate and muscle are displaced laterally as a unit: the posterior trunk of the mandibular nerve and the compartment's fat then come into view, and the poststyloid compartment lies deep to the styloid aponeurosis behind it. Tumours here most commonly arise from the deep lobe of the parotid gland (stated as background in the cadaver paper's Introduction).

structures.name: Poststyloid parapharyngeal compartment
structures.what: The posterior compartment of the parapharyngeal space, behind the fascia that runs back from the styloid process to the tensor veli palatini. It holds the internal carotid artery, the internal jugular vein and cranial nerves IX to XII (and, per the background text, the sympathetic chain).
structures.why: The neurovascular compartment: entering it endonasally by dissecting off the styloid aponeurosis exposes the ICA, the internal jugular vein and cranial nerves IX to XII. Tumours here usually arise from these neurovascular structures (stated as background in the cadaver paper's Introduction).

landmarks.name: Naris (nostril)
landmarks.locate: The nostril opening; the endoscope's fulcrum.

landmarks.name: Nasal sill
landmarks.locate: Midpoint of the floor of the nostril where vestibular skin meets the nasal floor; the zero point for intranasal distances.

landmarks.name: Anterior nasal spine
landmarks.locate: Anterior tip of the maxillary crest at the base of the columella.

landmarks.name: Anterior septal angle
landmarks.locate: Junction of the dorsal and caudal borders of the septal cartilage, the corner of the L-strut.

landmarks.name: Inferior turbinate head
landmarks.locate: Most anterior point of the inferior turbinate on the lateral wall, just behind the valve.

landmarks.name: Inferior turbinate tail
landmarks.locate: Most posterior point of the inferior turbinate, just in front of the choana.

landmarks.name: Middle turbinate axilla
landmarks.locate: Anterior-superior point where the middle turbinate joins the lateral nasal wall.

landmarks.name: Middle turbinate posterior attachment
landmarks.locate: Posterior end of the middle turbinate where it attaches to the lateral wall over the crista ethmoidalis, just anterior-inferior to the SPF.

landmarks.name: Maxillary natural ostium (centre)
landmarks.locate: Centre of the natural ostium in the floor of the ethmoidal infundibulum.

landmarks.name: Crista ethmoidalis
landmarks.locate: Most prominent point of the crista ethmoidalis on the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone.

landmarks.name: Sphenopalatine foramen (centre)
landmarks.locate: Centre of the SPF opening on the lateral nasal wall behind the crista ethmoidalis.

landmarks.name: Posterior septal artery on the sphenoid face
landmarks.locate: Point where the posterior septal artery crosses the midline of the anterior sphenoid face, between sphenoid ostium and choana.

landmarks.name: Eustachian tube orifice
landmarks.locate: Centre of the pharyngeal orifice of the Eustachian tube on the lateral nasopharyngeal wall.

landmarks.name: Valve of Hasner
landmarks.locate: Lower opening of the nasolacrimal duct high on the lateral wall of the inferior meatus.

landmarks.name: Upper end of nasolacrimal duct
landmarks.locate: Junction of lacrimal sac and nasolacrimal duct at the upper opening of the bony nasolacrimal canal.

landmarks.name: Lacrimal sac fundus
landmarks.locate: Highest point of the lacrimal sac, above the entry of the common canaliculus.

landmarks.name: Inferior orbital rim (above the foramen)
landmarks.locate: Point on the inferior orbital margin directly above the infraorbital foramen.

landmarks.name: Infraorbital foramen
landmarks.locate: Centre of the infraorbital foramen on the anterior maxilla.

landmarks.name: Canine fossa puncture site
landmarks.locate: Intersection of the mid-pupillary line with a horizontal line through the nasal floor (level of the nasal vestibule floor).

landmarks.name: Greater palatine foramen
landmarks.locate: Opening of the greater palatine canal on the posterolateral hard palate, medial to the upper 2nd–3rd molar.

landmarks.name: Vidian canal (anterior opening)
landmarks.locate: Anterior opening of the vidian canal in the posterior wall of the PPF, inferomedial to foramen rotundum.

landmarks.name: Foramen rotundum (anterior opening)
landmarks.locate: Anterior opening of foramen rotundum in the upper posterior wall of the PPF.

landmarks.name: Middle turbinate head
landmarks.locate: The anterior end of the middle turbinate. The septal projection of the turbinate's anterior attachment to the lateral wall (the axilla) is the anterior reference for the anterior ethmoidal artery's septal branch and a cut line for the short nasoseptal flap. The specimen landmark approximates the axilla with the turbinate's anterior end.

landmarks.name: Incisive canal, nasal opening
landmarks.locate: The nasal opening of the incisive canal, on the floor beside the septum's base.

variants.name: Concha bullosa
variants.def: Aerated middle turbinate on coronal CT; in strict use, pneumatisation of the bulbous (inferior) segment, alone or with the vertical lamella. Usually drains into the frontal recess or the retrobullar recess.
variants.why: A large one narrows the middle meatus, pushes the uncinate laterally and hides the OMC; lateral lamellectomy restores access. It can contain mucocele, polyps or be the site of the contact point in headache. Resect the lateral lamella: the medial lamella runs up to the skull-base attachment and is left. Treat the cell like an ethmoid cell — open it and preserve its mucosa; crushing it shrinks it only for a while and can trap its secretions.

prev.note: Counts any MT pneumatisation including lamellar. Other CT series report roughly 15–55%; the spread is mostly definition (lamellar counted or not) and per side vs per patient.

variants.name: Paradoxical middle turbinate
variants.def: Middle turbinate whose convexity faces laterally (towards the lateral nasal wall) instead of medially on coronal CT.
variants.why: Narrows the middle meatus and makes the MT likely to lateralise after surgery; consider conservative trimming of its inferior edge or a planned medialisation technique.

prev.note: Other series report substantially lower figures (often under 15%); the threshold for calling a curve paradoxical is not standardised.

variants.name: Infraorbital ethmoidal cell (Haller cell)
variants.def: Ethmoid cell pneumatising along the medial orbital floor (maxillary sinus roof) lateral to the infundibulum, below the lamina papyracea on coronal CT.
variants.why: A large cell narrows the infundibulum and maxillary ostium from above and laterally; it must be opened (from the antrostomy or infundibulum) and its roof is the orbit. Reaching it usually needs angled scopes and angled (90°, giraffe) forceps.

prev.note: Counts any cell along the orbital floor, including small ones. Series using a stricter definition (cells large enough to narrow the infundibulum) report much lower rates (single digits to about 20%); this is the main reason studies disagree.

variants.name: Accessory maxillary ostium
variants.def: Additional opening of the maxillary sinus through the (usually posterior) fontanelle, separate from and posterior-inferior to the natural ostium, visible without removing the uncinate.
variants.why: It is not the natural ostium: an antrostomy that enlarges only the accessory opening leaves two openings and mucus recirculates out of the natural ostium and back in. Join it to the natural ostium.

prev.note: Wide spread across cadaver and endoscopic series; some accessory ostia are acquired (post-inflammatory) rather than developmental, and endoscopic series miss ostia hidden by the uncinate.

variants.name: Pneumatised uncinate process (uncinate bulla)
variants.def: Air cell within the superior (vertical) part of the uncinate process on coronal CT, usually an extension of the agger nasi cell.
variants.why: Can narrow the infundibulum and frontal recess; remove it with the uncinate and agger nasi.

variants.name: Uncinate inserting on the lamina papyracea
variants.def: Superior uncinate curves laterally to insert on the lamina papyracea, closing the infundibulum above as a recessus terminalis.
variants.why: The frontal sinus then drains medial to the uncinate into the middle meatus; the top of the uncinate is on the orbit, so cut it from medial with a through-cutter.

variants.name: Uncinate inserting on the skull base
variants.def: Superior uncinate runs straight up to insert on the ethmoid roof.
variants.why: The frontal sinus drains into the infundibulum. Twisting the upper uncinate can fracture the skull base; cut it, and remove the top only while you can see the frontal recess.

variants.name: Uncinate inserting on the middle turbinate
variants.def: Superior uncinate bends medially to insert on the middle turbinate.
variants.why: Frontal drainage runs into the infundibulum, so infundibular disease can obstruct the frontal sinus; release the uncinate from the MT without destabilising the turbinate.

variants.name: Chronic maxillary atelectasis (silent sinus syndrome)
variants.def: Acquired loss of maxillary sinus volume with inward bowing of the walls behind an occluded ostium: on CT, small opacified sinus, depressed orbital floor, uncinate lateralised against the orbit, enlarged middle meatus. Silent sinus syndrome = spontaneous painless enophthalmos/hypoglobus from it.
variants.why: The uncinate lies on the orbit and the orbital floor is thin and low: uncinectomy and antrostomy carry high orbital risk. Treat with careful uncinectomy/antrostomy; orbital floor repair is staged if needed.

variants.name: Maxillary sinus hypoplasia
variants.def: Congenitally small maxillary sinus with thick walls, often with a hypoplastic or absent uncinate and a lateralised infundibulum.
variants.why: Easy to misread as opacified or diseased; the orbit is closer to the middle meatus than expected, so uncinectomy must stay medial.

variants.name: Maxillary sinus septa (Underwood septa)
variants.def: Bony septa rising from the floor or walls of the maxillary sinus, partly or completely dividing it into recesses.
variants.why: Disease can be trapped behind a septum after a normal antrostomy; they matter for sinus lift and implant surgery.

prev.note: 30 septa counted in 90 sinuses, so strictly septa per sinus rather than affected sinuses. Modern CT/CBCT series vary widely with the minimum height counted as a septum and whether patients are dentate.

variants.name: Septal deviation
variants.def: Departure of the septum from the midline, cartilaginous, bony or both; describe by site (valve area vs posterior) and shape ([[c.mladina-septal]]).
variants.why: Obstructs the airway (mainly at the valve) and the surgical corridor (posteriorly); a deviation that blocks the middle meatus should be corrected before or during FESS. Some deviation is present in most people (textbook estimates of about 77–90% of the general population), so treat the deviation that explains the symptoms or blocks the route, not one that is merely visible.

variants.name: Septal spur
variants.def: Sharp horizontal bony or osteocartilaginous projection, usually along the vomer–maxillary crest junction, often touching the IT or lateral wall.
variants.why: Blocks scope passage and can cause contact-point pain; mucosa over it is thin, so elevate from above and below towards it and remove it with a chisel or through-cutting instrument.

variants.name: Sphenopalatine artery with multiple branches
variants.def: The SPA divides into two or more branches before or at the SPF, so several vessels emerge medial to the crista ethmoidalis.
