variants.why: Clipping the first vessel seen is not enough: search behind and below the crista for every branch, including the posterior septal artery, or epistaxis recurs.

prev.note: Two or more branches medial to the crista in 73 of 75 cadaver specimens; three or more in 67% and four or more in 35%; a single trunk in only 2 specimens.

variants.name: Accessory (double) sphenopalatine foramen
variants.def: Two separate openings in place of a single SPF, one into the superior and one into the middle meatus (Wareing class III), each able to transmit SPA branches.
variants.why: A branch through a second foramen is missed by ligation at the main foramen; explore the lateral wall around it.

prev.note: Osteological series (35% opened only into the superior meatus, 56% spanned both meati, 9% had two openings). Soft-tissue dissections of branch patterns are more relevant clinically, and small accessory foramina for branches are not counted here.

Textbook-reported, primary study not named: the SPA had branched before leaving the foramen, its branches passing through separate bony openings. This looser definition (any separate branch foramen) likely explains the gap from the 9% of true double foramina in dry skulls.

variants.name: Suspended (protruding) infraorbital canal
variants.def: On coronal CT the infraorbital canal hangs below the antral roof on a bony septum, with the nerve partly in the sinus lumen; the canal wall may be dehiscent.
variants.why: Debriders and angled instruments in the antral roof or a large Haller cell can injure the nerve directly.

prev.note: Canal fully descended into the lumen (type 3); a further 27.0% of nerves lay below the roof but juxtaposed to it (type 2). Commoner with an ipsilateral infraorbital ethmoid (Haller) cell. Series that count per patient, or count any protrusion, report different rates: check definition and denominator before comparing.

variants.name: V2 prominence in the lateral sphenoid recess
variants.def: With lateral recess pneumatisation, foramen rotundum/V2 bulges into the lateral sphenoid wall, sometimes with a dehiscent bony covering.
variants.why: A landmark for the lateral recess and Meckel's cave, and a nerve at risk when disease is removed from the lateral recess.

variants.name: Choanal atresia
variants.def: Congenital obstruction of the choana, most often mixed bony-membranous; CT shows a narrowed posterior nasal cavity, a thickened vomer and medial bowing of the lateral nasal wall.
variants.why: Bilateral atresia is a neonatal airway emergency; unilateral presents later with one-sided discharge. Repair endoscopically by removing the atretic plate and the posterior vomer ([[p.choanal-atresia-repair]]).

variants.name: Level at which the posterior septal artery divides
variants.why: A branch point on the sphenoid face puts two vessels, not one, in the strip between the sphenoid ostium and the choanal arch.

prev.note: close to the sphenopalatine foramen; the other 34.6% divided at the posterior border of the nasal septum
5 of 7 sides divided on the rostrum lateral to the sphenoid ostium and 2 medial to it; very small series, a different landmark from the one above

variants.def: Whether the artery divides into its two septal branches close to the sphenopalatine foramen or later, at the posterior border of the septum.

variants.name: Two septal artery branches in the flap pedicle
variants.why: The commoner finding: the pedicle should be treated as two vessels, and the distance from the artery to the sphenoid ostium (about 9 mm, [[m.psa-to-sphenoid-ostium]]) as the margin to protect.

prev.note: dissection after endoscopic craniofacial resection; the denominator is not given in the abstract

variants.def: Two branches of the septal artery found in the pedicle of a raised nasoseptal flap.

variants.name: Inferior branch dominant
variants.why: The dominant branch always lay below the axial plane of the sphenoid ostium in the same series, so an inferior sphenoidotomy margin is where it is most exposed.
variants.def: The inferior septal branch is the larger of the two.

variants.name: Two or three sphenopalatine arterial trunks
variants.why: A clip or cautery on one trunk leaves flow in the others, which is why sphenopalatine ligation fails when a trunk is missed; look for an accessory foramen too.
variants.def: More than one arterial trunk leaves the sphenopalatine foramen.

variants.name: Source of the nasal tip's main supply
variants.why: Whichever it is, the alar arcade connects them; the variant matters when the tip skin is raised or a pedicled flap is planned.

prev.note: the lateral nasal artery in 78% of sides and the dorsal nasal in 22%; a single Asian population, not generalizable

variants.def: Which artery is the main source of the nasal tip: the lateral nasal (facial) or the dorsal nasal (ophthalmic).

classifications.name: Superior attachment of the uncinate process (Landsberg–Friedman)
classifications.basis: Site of the superior (vertical) insertion of the uncinate process on coronal/sagittal CT, which determines whether the frontal sinus drainage pathway opens medial to the uncinate (middle meatus) or into the ethmoidal infundibulum.

classes.label: Lamina papyracea
classes.criterion: Uncinate inserts laterally on the lamina papyracea.
classes.why: The infundibulum ends blindly in a [[s.recessus-terminalis]]; the frontal sinus drains medial to the uncinate into the middle meatus.

classes.label: Agger nasi (posteromedial wall)
classes.criterion: Uncinate inserts on the posteromedial wall of the [[s.agger-nasi-cell]].
classes.why: Frontal drainage passes medial to the uncinate; the uncinate top and agger nasi are removed together in frontal recess surgery.

classes.label: Lamina papyracea and MT–cribriform junction
classes.criterion: Dual insertion: lamina papyracea and the junction of the middle turbinate with the cribriform plate.

classes.label: MT–cribriform junction
classes.criterion: Uncinate inserts at the junction of the middle turbinate with the cribriform plate.
classes.why: Frontal drainage enters the infundibulum; dissection at the top of the uncinate is close to the lateral lamella.

classes.label: Skull base
classes.criterion: Uncinate inserts directly on the ethmoid roof.
classes.why: Frontal drainage enters the infundibulum; pulling the uncinate top can fracture the skull base, so cut it.

classes.label: Middle turbinate
classes.criterion: Uncinate bends medially to insert on the middle turbinate.
classes.why: Frontal drainage enters the infundibulum; infundibular disease can obstruct the frontal sinus.

classifications.caveats: Many texts simplify to three sites (lamina papyracea, skull base, middle turbinate), and the uncinate may insert at more than one site. The practical point is lateral (types 1–2, drainage medial to the uncinate) versus medial/superior (types 4–6, drainage into the infundibulum). Prevalence per type varies between series and is not given here; lamina papyracea insertion is generally reported as the most common.

classifications.name: Middle turbinate pneumatisation (Bolger)
classifications.basis: Which part of the middle turbinate is aerated on coronal CT.

classes.label: Lamellar
classes.criterion: Pneumatisation confined to the vertical lamella (attachment) of the MT, not the bulbous inferior part.
classes.why: Rarely obstructive; often called lamellar concha, not a true concha bullosa.

classes.label: Bulbous
classes.criterion: Pneumatisation of the inferior bulbous segment only.
classes.why: Can narrow the middle meatus and push the uncinate laterally.

classes.label: Extensive
classes.criterion: Both the vertical lamella and the bulbous segment are pneumatised.
classes.why: Most likely to obstruct the OMC and limit access; treated by lateral lamellectomy (crushing is an alternative).

classifications.caveats: Concha bullosa in clinical use usually means bulbous or extensive pneumatisation; prevalence figures depend on whether lamellar pneumatisation is counted.

classifications.name: Mladina classification of septal deformity
classifications.basis: Shape and position of the septal deformity on anterior rhinoscopy/endoscopy: vertical deformities in the valve area or deeper, horizontal spurs, and combinations.

classes.label: Mild vertical ridge, valve area
classes.criterion: Unilateral vertical ridge in the valve area not touching the lateral wall.

classes.label: Vertical ridge touching the valve
classes.criterion: Unilateral vertical ridge in the valve area that touches the lateral wall.

classes.label: Deep vertical deformity
classes.criterion: Unilateral vertical deformity further back, at the level of the MT head.

classes.label: S-shaped
classes.criterion: Type 2 or 3 on one side and a deformity on the other side at a different depth.

classes.label: Horizontal spur, one side
classes.criterion: Unilateral horizontal basal spur; the opposite side is flat.

classes.label: Spur with contralateral gutter
classes.criterion: Type 5 plus a deep gutter on the concave side.

classes.label: Combined
classes.criterion: Combination of more than one of types 1–6.

classifications.caveats: Descriptive and widely used in research; inter-observer agreement is moderate and it does not grade severity. Types 1–2 matter for airflow (valve), types 3, 5–7 more for surgical access.

classifications.name: Infraorbital canal configuration
classifications.basis: Relationship of the infraorbital canal to the maxillary sinus roof on coronal CT.

classes.label: Within the roof
classes.criterion: Canal entirely within the bony orbital floor/antral roof.

classes.label: Bulging
classes.criterion: Canal partly protrudes below the roof into the sinus lumen.

classes.label: Suspended
classes.criterion: Canal descends into the sinus, hanging from the roof on a bony septum or mesentery.
classes.why: The nerve is exposed in the lumen and easily injured by debriders and angled instruments; flag it before any maxillary sinus surgery.

classifications.caveats: Several numbering schemes exist in the literature; confirm which one a paper uses before comparing prevalences. Associated with infraorbital ethmoid (Haller) cells and larger sinuses.

classifications.name: Prelacrimal recess (anterior maxillary wall–NLD distance)
classifications.basis: Axial CT distance between the anterior maxillary wall and the anterior margin of the bony nasolacrimal canal at the level of the inferior turbinate.

classes.label: Narrow
classes.criterion: Distance under 3 mm.
classes.why: A prelacrimal window needs extensive anterior wall removal and NLD displacement; consider other routes.

classes.label: Intermediate
classes.criterion: Distance 3–7 mm.

classes.label: Wide
classes.criterion: Distance over 7 mm.

classifications.caveats: Thresholds from one CT series of 200 sides, which found type I in 31.5%, type II in 56.5% and type III in only 12.5%: a wide recess is the exception. Later series differ in the axial level measured; measure both sides, as it is often asymmetric.

classifications.name: Maxillary sinus hypoplasia (Bolger)
classifications.basis: CT degree of maxillary sinus hypoplasia and the associated development of the uncinate process and infundibulum.

classes.label: Mild
classes.criterion: Mildly hypoplastic sinus, normal uncinate, well-developed infundibulum.

classes.label: Significant
classes.criterion: Significant hypoplasia; uncinate hypoplastic or absent and lateralised against the orbit; infundibulum poorly defined.
classes.why: The uncinate lies on the lamina papyracea: uncinectomy risks orbital entry.

classes.label: Profound
classes.criterion: Profound, cleft-like hypoplasia with absent uncinate.
classes.why: There is little sinus to open; the orbit is immediately lateral to the middle meatus.

classifications.caveats: Distinguish congenital hypoplasia from acquired atelectasis (silent sinus), in which the sinus shrinks and the walls are drawn inwards.

classifications.name: Vidian canal position relative to the sphenoid floor
classifications.basis: Coronal CT: where the vidian canal lies relative to the floor of the sphenoid sinus.

classes.label: Protruding
classes.criterion: Canal lies above the floor, projecting into the sinus.
classes.why: Easiest to find from inside the sphenoid, and easiest to injure while flattening the floor.

classes.label: On the floor
classes.criterion: Canal lies on the floor, partly protruding into the sinus.
classes.why: Usually still visible as a ridge in the floor.

classes.label: Embedded
classes.criterion: Canal lies within the bone of the floor or sphenoid body, below the sinus.
classes.why: Not seen from the sinus; reach it from the PPF or by drilling the floor.

classifications.caveats: Criteria as summarised in a surgical atlas chapter; check the primary CT study's exact definitions before using the boundary between types 1 and 2 for research.

classifications.name: Yenigun axial-CT classification of the infraorbital canal
classifications.basis: Position of the infraorbital canal relative to the maxillary sinus on axial CT in 750 patients (Yenigun et al. 2016). Its numbering runs the opposite way to [[c.infraorbital-canal]]: here type 1 is the most protruding canal, so the same number means a different canal in the two schemes.

classes.label: Totally protruding into the sinus
classes.criterion: The infraorbital canal is totally protruding into the maxillary sinus.
classes.why: Occurred together with maxillary sinus septa (significant on both sides); the protruded canal was twice as frequent, 25%, when septa were present.

classes.label: At the sinus floor or partly protruding
classes.criterion: The infraorbital canal is located at the floor of the maxillary sinus or is partially protruding into the maxillary sinus.

classes.label: Embedded in the maxilla or bulging on its outer face
classes.criterion: The infraorbital canal is totally embedded in the maxillary corpus or is bulging on the external face of the maxillary sinus.

classifications.caveats: Do not map types across schemes by number. Roughly, Yenigun Y1 corresponds to the most protruding (descended, 'suspended') type of [[c.infraorbital-canal]] and Y3 to the canal within the bone, but Y2 here also includes a canal lying at the sinus floor and Y3 includes a canal bulging on the outer maxillary face, which the three-type scheme does not describe. Acar et al. 2018 (200 patients, multidetector CT) used four types: within the maxillary bony roof, partly protruding, within the sinus, and at the outer limit of the zygomatic recess; a systematic review (Orellana-Donoso 2024) pooled the literature into four variants with a different fourth type (in the orbital floor), so published schemes differ in both number of types and numbering. The abstracts do not state whether prevalences are per patient or per side, so none is quoted here.

measurements.name: Nasolacrimal duct length
measurements.what: Length of the nasolacrimal duct from the lower end of the lacrimal sac to the valve of Hasner.
measurements.note: The bony canal accounts for most of it; the lower meatal part varies with where the duct opens under the IT.

measurements.name: Lacrimal sac height
measurements.what: Vertical length of the lacrimal sac from fundus to the start of the nasolacrimal duct.

measurements.name: Lacrimal sac extension above the MT axilla
measurements.what: How far the lacrimal sac fundus lies above the axilla of the middle turbinate.
measurements.note: The finding that most of the sac lies above the axilla changed endoscopic DCR: bone must be removed well above the axilla, not only around the duct.

measurements.name: Nasolacrimal duct to maxillary natural ostium
measurements.what: Anteroposterior distance from the anterior margin of the maxillary natural ostium to the nasolacrimal duct in front of it.
measurements.note: Commonly quoted surgical figure; published direct measurements are few and vary with where the ostium lies. The point is that there are only millimetres to spare anteriorly.

measurements.name: Valve of Hasner behind the IT head
measurements.what: Distance from the anterior end of the inferior turbinate back to the nasolacrimal duct opening in the inferior meatus.
measurements.note: Approximate textbook figure; the opening position varies. Inferior meatal work should start behind it.

measurements.name: Infraorbital foramen below the orbital rim
measurements.what: Vertical distance from the inferior orbital rim down to the infraorbital foramen.
measurements.note: Varies with sex and population; the foramen is about 1 cm below the rim in most adults.

measurements.name: Eustachian tube orifice behind the IT tail
measurements.what: Distance from the posterior end of the inferior turbinate to the pharyngeal orifice of the Eustachian tube.

measurements.name: Greater palatine canal length
measurements.what: Length of the greater (descending) palatine canal from the greater palatine foramen to the PPF.
measurements.note: Reported means depend on where the canal is said to end: about 18–19 mm when measured only to the floor of the PPF, about 31 mm in a large CT series measured further up to the PPF. The transpalatal injection rule (needle bent 25 mm from the tip at 45°) was derived from the shorter measurement plus palatal soft tissue; limiting depth keeps the tip out of the orbit via the inferior orbital fissure.

measurements.name: Vidian canal length
measurements.what: Length of the pterygoid (vidian) canal from its posterior end at the foramen lacerum to its anterior opening in the PPF.
measurements.note: Reported means differ between cadaver and CT series and by where the posterior end is defined (lacerum vs petrous ICA genu).

measurements.name: Septal L-strut width to preserve
measurements.what: Minimum width of dorsal and caudal septal cartilage left in septoplasty to preserve nasal support.
measurements.note: The 10 mm rule is a convention; engineering analysis suggests a wider strut (or reinforcement) where cartilage is thin, and the dorsal strut near the keystone is most important. A current surgical atlas chapter sets 15 mm as the minimum; the 10–15 mm range reflects differing conventions, not conflicting measurements.

measurements.name: Nasoseptal flap superior incision below the skull base
measurements.what: Distance below the top of the septum (cribriform plate) at which the superior NSF incision runs, to spare the olfactory epithelium.
measurements.note: Technique descriptions place it 1–2 cm below and parallel to the top of the septum; the principle is to keep the uppermost septal mucosa (olfactory strip) in place. One cribriform-repair chapter accepts a superior incision as close as 5 mm below the skull base when the flap must reach a cribriform defect: more flap height for more olfactory risk (practice variation, not a new default).

measurements.name: Maxillary sinus volume
measurements.what: Air volume of one adult maxillary sinus.
measurements.note: Wide spread with age, sex, dentition and population; hypoplastic and atelectatic sinuses are much smaller.

measurements.name: Endoscopic SPA ligation success
measurements.what: Proportion of patients with refractory posterior epistaxis controlled by endoscopic SPA ligation/cauterisation.
measurements.note: Pooled from uncontrolled case series with short follow-up and likely publication bias, so real-world rebleeding is higher. Failures relate to missed branches (posterior septal artery, second foramen) and an unrecognised anterior ethmoidal source.
measurements.population: patients with refractory posterior epistaxis in 11 early case series

measurements.name: Nasal sill to sphenopalatine foramen
measurements.what: Straight-line distance from the nasal sill to the sphenopalatine foramen.
measurements.note: Endoscopic cadaver dissection in a small series; the spread is wide, so distance alone does not find the foramen: use the MT tail and the crista ethmoidalis. The SPF lies just anterior to the sphenoid face, a little short of the sphenoid ostium distance.

measurements.name: Septal artery to sphenoid ostium
measurements.what: Distance between the posterior septal artery on the sphenoid face and the sphenoid ostium.
measurements.note: A single mean from one dissection-and-CT study; the abstract gives no spread or n for the dissections. Compare with the chart distance in the specimen.

measurements.name: Nasoseptal flap area against defect area
measurements.what: Area of the harvested nasoseptal flap measured in an anatomical and radiological study; the anterior skull base defects in the same series averaged 8.64 cm².
measurements.population: 30 CT scans compared; flap and defect measured on cadaver dissection and CT
measurements.note: The flap was larger than the defect in all cases, but the anterior edge was the margin most likely to fall short (difference in width 5 mm or less in a third). The abstract does not say which design (short, full) this is. The atlas chapter on large defect reconstruction (Table 31.2) quotes about 25.1 cm² as the maximum nasoseptal flap area in a radioanatomic study (Pinheiro-Neto 2007), and says Asian nasal cavities may not offer the same septal mucosal area as those of white patients.

measurements.name: Extended nasoseptal flap: added length and area
measurements.what: What adding the nasal floor and inferior meatus mucosa gives over a standard flap: about 20 mm more length and 774 mm² more area.
measurements.note: Value shown is the added length in mm; the added area is about 774 mm². The extended flap covered a clival defect from tuberculum to foramen magnum in 66.6% and from below the sella in 91.6%; a defect lateral to the hypoglossal canals is unlikely to be covered.

measurements.name: Bipedicled anterior septal flap: length and area
measurements.what: Length from the incisive canal to the sphenoid face at the level of the choanal arch, as the long axis of the bipedicled anterior septal flap. Mean area 916.46 ± 262.66 mm².
measurements.population: 9 midline sagittal CT images; confirmed in 4 cadavers
measurements.note: The same series puts the flap's coverage at about 100% of the frontal beak and 51% of the posterior frontal table. Pedicles: the septal branch of the superior labial artery and the nasopalatine artery.

measurements.name: Middle turbinate flap area
measurements.what: Mean surface area of the middle turbinate flap; flaps shorter than 4.0 cm did not reach the sella.
measurements.note: Covered planum and fovea defects in all 12 flaps; 2 of 12 could not cover a sellar defect. Technically demanding. The atlas quotes the same mean (5.6 cm²) and stresses that dimensions vary with turbinate size.

measurements.name: Anterior ethmoidal artery septal entry behind the middle turbinate axilla
measurements.what: On a sagittal plane, the distance from the septal projection of the middle turbinate's anterior attachment back to the vertical line through the entry of the anterior ethmoidal artery into the septum.
measurements.population: 10 nasal cavities of 5 adult cadaveric heads (CT)
measurements.note: Basis for a unilateral septal flap on the septal branch of the anterior ethmoidal artery. Measured from the axilla, which the specimen landmark approximates with the turbinate head.

measurements.name: Internal nasal valve angle
measurements.what: The angle between the septum and the lateral wall at the internal valve. 10 to 15 degrees is the paper's hypothesised true value; standard coronal CT sections read it wider than a section reformatted through the valve.
measurements.population: 24 rhinoplasty patients with CT for nasal obstruction
measurements.note: The paper tests a reformatting plane against the hypothesised true value; it does not establish a normal range, and no correlation with the modified Cottle maneuver was found.

measurements.name: Supraorbital artery: axial vascularization of the pericranial flap
measurements.what: Length of pericranium reliably vascularized along the supraorbital artery; the supratrochlear artery gave 35 ± 10.4 mm.
measurements.note: Superficial dissection should end 15 mm above the orbital rim to keep the flap alive; the deep and superficial branches divide a median 8 mm above the rim. A nasal reconstruction series, small n.

measurements.name: Inferior turbinate pedicle flap: length
measurements.what: Length of the posterior pedicle inferior turbinate flap raised in nine cadaver heads.
measurements.note: Width of the distal third 22.1 ± 3.7 mm. Reach 112 ± 21 % of the posterior cranial fossa length and 67 ± 10 % of the anterior cranial fossa length (the abstract gives ± 9.9).

measurements.name: Inferior turbinate flap: maximum area
measurements.what: Approximate maximum surface area of the posterior pedicle inferior turbinate flap, as tabulated in the atlas chapter.
measurements.note: Table 31.2 of the atlas chapter cites Harvey 2009 (its ref. 47) for 2.4 cm², which Harvey's own dimensions ([[m.itf-dimensions]]) contradict. The printed table confirms "2.4" with ref. 47, so the inconsistency is the atlas's. Unresolved until the primary source of the figure is found. The primary report on this flap (Fortes 2007) is a four-patient series whose abstract gives no area.

hazards.name: Orbital entry during uncinectomy
hazards.site: Lateral wall of the infundibulum, immediately behind a lateralised uncinate.
hazards.mechanism: Sickle knife or back-biter driven laterally through the uncinate into the lamina papyracea, especially with an atelectatic sinus, maxillary sinus hypoplasia or a uncinate lying on the orbit; microdebrider suction then draws orbital fat in.
hazards.consequence: Orbital fat herniation, medial rectus injury (diplopia), orbital haematoma; rarely visual loss.
hazards.prevent: Review coronal CT for uncinate position and sinus size; palpate behind the uncinate with a ball probe; cut parallel to the orbit with instruments pointed medially; prefer a swing-door or back-biter technique; turn the debrider off near the lamina.
hazards.recognize: Yellow fat that does not sink and that moves with gentle globe pressure (ballottement); a dehiscence seen in the lateral infundibulum; periorbital bruising or proptosis.
hazards.rescue: Stop debriding there; leave fat alone (do not pull or cauterise), avoid packing, and finish elsewhere carefully. Check eye movements and pupil; for rising pressure (proptosis, tense orbit) do lateral canthotomy/cantholysis and consider endoscopic medial decompression; urgent ophthalmology if muscle injury suspected.

hazards.name: Nasolacrimal duct injury
hazards.site: Anterior margin of the antrostomy, in the bony nasolacrimal canal just in front of the natural ostium.
hazards.mechanism: Back-biting or punching forward through the hard bone of the nasolacrimal canal when enlarging the antrostomy anteriorly; crushing or tearing the duct in medial maxillectomy.
hazards.consequence: Epiphora and dacryocystitis; many injuries are subclinical because the duct drains into the antrostomy.
hazards.prevent: Enlarge posteriorly and inferiorly, not anteriorly; stop when bone becomes hard; in maxillectomy or prelacrimal work, divide the duct sharply and obliquely instead of avulsing it.
hazards.recognize: Hard bone giving way at the anterior antrostomy margin; a white tubular structure; post-op epiphora.
hazards.rescue: A cleanly transected duct that opens into the antrostomy often drains; persistent epiphora is treated by endoscopic DCR. In planned transection, marsupialise the cut duct; some add a DCR at the same sitting to prevent stenosis — the steps of a formal DCR (remove the remaining lacrimal bone, cannulate and slit the duct vertically, evert its mucosa), usually without stents.

hazards.name: Missed natural ostium and mucus recirculation
hazards.site: Middle meatus: antrostomy made through the posterior fontanelle or an accessory ostium while the natural ostium stays hidden behind an uncinate remnant.
hazards.mechanism: Incomplete uncinectomy; mistaking an accessory ostium for the natural ostium; mucociliary flow continues toward the natural ostium and re-enters the sinus through the separate surgical opening.
hazards.consequence: Persistent maxillary sinusitis despite a patent-looking antrostomy (recirculation), a common cause of revision surgery.
hazards.prevent: Remove the uncinate completely; find the natural ostium with a 30°/45° scope and ball probe; join any accessory ostium or fontanelle opening to the natural ostium into one antrostomy.
hazards.recognize: Two separate openings; mucus seen leaving one opening and entering the other; uncinate remnant in the anterior middle meatus.
hazards.rescue: Revise: remove the uncinate remnant and connect the openings into one.

hazards.name: Bleeding from posterior extension of the antrostomy
hazards.site: Posterior margin of the antrostomy and the MT tail region, near the SPF.
hazards.mechanism: Extending the antrostomy posteriorly to the palatine bone divides branches of the posterior lateral nasal artery.
hazards.consequence: Brisk arterial bleeding that obscures the field and may present as post-op epistaxis.
hazards.prevent: Stop the posterior antrostomy at the posterior wall of the sinus; coagulate before extending near the palatine bone.
hazards.recognize: Pulsatile bleed from the posterior antrostomy edge.
hazards.rescue: Suction-bipolar or suction cautery; if it retracts, raise a flap to the crista ethmoidalis and control the SPA branch.

hazards.name: Infraorbital nerve injury
hazards.site: Antral roof, especially over a suspended or dehiscent infraorbital canal or a large Haller cell; V2 in the PPF.
hazards.mechanism: Curved debrider or angled forceps stripping the roof; drilling or retracting in the upper PPF.
hazards.consequence: Cheek, upper lip and lower lid numbness, sometimes painful dysaesthesia.
hazards.prevent: Identify the canal on coronal CT ([[c.infraorbital-canal]]); keep debriders off the roof ridge; in the PPF, dissect the nerve in the neural plane under vision.
hazards.recognize: Exposed white nerve on the antral roof; post-op sensory loss.
hazards.rescue: Nothing to repair endoscopically; counsel and follow; most neuropraxias recover.

hazards.name: Anterior superior alveolar nerve injury
hazards.site: Anterior maxillary wall, medial part of the canine fossa and around the piriform aperture.
hazards.mechanism: Trephine or window placed too medially or too high; drilling the anterior wall.
hazards.consequence: Numb or painful upper incisors, canine and lip; usually temporary, occasionally permanent dysaesthesia.
hazards.prevent: Place the canine fossa puncture at the intersection of the mid-pupillary line and the nasal-floor line ([[lm.canine-fossa-puncture]]); limit anterior drilling in prelacrimal approaches.
hazards.recognize: Post-op dental or lip numbness.
hazards.rescue: Reassure and follow; symptomatic management of dysaesthesia.

hazards.name: Oroantral fistula
hazards.site: Sublabial incision and anterior wall/floor of the maxillary sinus.
hazards.mechanism: Breakdown of the sublabial wound over a large anterior wall window (Caldwell-Luc), or opening the floor near dental roots.
hazards.consequence: Persistent communication between mouth and antrum with fluid regurgitation and sinusitis.
hazards.prevent: Keep the sublabial incision well above the gingival sulcus, the window small, and close in layers; clear the ostiomeatal drainage.
hazards.recognize: Air or fluid passing between mouth and nose; a visible fistula in the buccal sulcus.
hazards.rescue: Treat sinusitis and ensure antrostomy drainage; small fistulae may close; persistent ones need local (buccal advancement or palatal) flap closure.

hazards.name: Septal perforation
hazards.site: Cartilaginous septum, typically where flaps were torn on both sides or where cartilage was left bare.
hazards.mechanism: Opposing mucoperichondrial tears, bilateral cautery, septal haematoma or abscess, or leaving the contralateral mucosa over resected cartilage unsupported after NSF harvest.
hazards.consequence: Crusting, bleeding, whistling and, if large, loss of support.
hazards.prevent: Stay subperichondrial; repair tears; avoid opposing tears; replace straightened cartilage between the flaps; splints; after NSF harvest, keep the contralateral mucosa and cartilage intact or cover the donor site.
hazards.recognize: Tears seen at the end of the procedure; crusting and a hole at follow-up.
hazards.rescue: Intraoperatively, close one side and interpose cartilage or fascia; established perforations are managed with saline and emollients, a button, or flap repair.

hazards.name: Septal haematoma
hazards.site: Between the mucoperichondrial flaps.
hazards.mechanism: Bleeding into the dead space left after elevation, without quilting, splints or drainage.
hazards.consequence: Cartilage necrosis and abscess leading to perforation and saddle deformity.
hazards.prevent: Haemostasis, quilting sutures and/or splints; leave a drainage path in the flap.
hazards.recognize: Bilateral boggy septal swelling and blockage in the first days, often painful.
hazards.rescue: Urgent incision and drainage, re-quilting or packing, and antibiotics.

hazards.name: Loss of septal support (saddle nose)
hazards.site: Dorsal and caudal L-strut and the keystone area.
hazards.mechanism: Resecting too much of the dorsal strut, disarticulating the keystone, or fracturing the strut while straightening.
hazards.consequence: Dorsal depression, tip ptosis and columellar retraction.
hazards.prevent: Preserve at least 10–15 mm of dorsal and caudal strut ([[m.l-strut-width]]); cut, do not twist, at the bony–cartilaginous junction; never detach cartilage from the nasal bones.
hazards.recognize: Loss of dorsal support on palpation at the end of surgery; visible deformity later.
hazards.rescue: Reinforce with spreader or batten grafts or suture to the nasal spine; established deformity needs open reconstruction.

hazards.name: Skull base fracture from the perpendicular plate
hazards.site: Junction of the perpendicular plate with the cribriform plate.
hazards.mechanism: Twisting or rocking the perpendicular plate transmits force to the cribriform plate.
hazards.consequence: CSF rhinorrhoea, meningitis risk, anosmia.
hazards.prevent: Cut the perpendicular plate with through-cutting forceps below the skull base; never twist.
hazards.recognize: Clear fluid after the manoeuvre; post-op unilateral watery rhinorrhoea (beta-2 transferrin).
hazards.rescue: Identify and repair the defect endoscopically (graft plus mucosal flap); see [[p.csf-leak-repair]].

hazards.name: Empty nose syndrome after turbinate over-resection
hazards.site: Inferior (and middle) turbinate mucosa.
hazards.mechanism: Radical turbinectomy or extensive mucosal destruction removes the tissue that senses and conditions airflow.
hazards.consequence: Paradoxical sensation of obstruction, dryness, crusting and distress despite a wide cavity.
hazards.prevent: Reduce submucosally, preserve the medial mucosa, and out-fracture instead of resecting.
hazards.recognize: Late complaint of obstruction or suffocation with a very wide cavity on endoscopy; cotton test relieves symptoms.
hazards.rescue: Humidification and emollients; submucosal implants to rebuild the turbinate in selected patients.

hazards.name: Posterior bleeding after turbinate reduction
hazards.site: Posterior end of the inferior turbinate.
hazards.mechanism: Resection or submucosal debridement of the IT tail divides the inferior turbinate branch of the posterior lateral nasal artery.
hazards.consequence: Early or delayed (sloughing at 7–10 days) posterior epistaxis.
hazards.prevent: Limit posterior resection; coagulate the tail under endoscopic vision.
hazards.recognize: Blood running into the nasopharynx; bleeding point at the IT tail on endoscopy.
hazards.rescue: Endoscopic cautery of the tail; if uncontrolled, SPA ligation ([[p.spa-ligation]]).

hazards.name: Middle turbinate lateralisation and synechia
hazards.site: Middle meatus between the MT and the lateral wall.
hazards.mechanism: Fracture or destabilisation of the MT (especially of its basal lamella or axilla) and opposing raw mucosal surfaces.
hazards.consequence: Scar closure of the middle meatus and OMC, with recurrent maxillary, ethmoid and frontal disease.
hazards.prevent: Do not grasp or fracture the MT; preserve its axilla and basal lamella; medialise with a Bolgerisation (controlled scar to the septum), suture or spacer; early debridement.
hazards.recognize: MT adherent to the lateral wall at post-op endoscopy.
hazards.rescue: Divide adhesions early in clinic; revise with medialisation or conservative partial MT resection.

hazards.name: Rebleeding after SPA ligation
hazards.site: SPF and the posterior septal branch on the sphenoid face.
hazards.mechanism: Only one of several SPA branches controlled (the others lie behind or below the crista, or exit an accessory foramen); posterior septal artery not addressed; bleeding actually from the anterior ethmoidal artery.
hazards.consequence: Recurrent epistaxis needing repeat surgery or embolisation.
hazards.prevent: Remove the crista ethmoidalis; identify and clip or cauterise every branch; also cauterise the posterior septal artery on the sphenoid face; consider AEA ligation when bleeding is superior.
hazards.recognize: Rebleeding within days; endoscopy locates the source.
hazards.rescue: Re-explore and control missed branches; add AEA ligation or IMAX embolisation (mind ICA–ECA anastomoses).

hazards.name: Posterior septal artery haemorrhage
hazards.site: Anterior sphenoid face between the sphenoid ostium and the choana.
hazards.mechanism: Inferior extension of a sphenoidotomy (including a drill-out, a radical sphenoidectomy or the sphenoidotomy of an optic nerve decompression) or a posterior septectomy divides the artery; in clinic, an adherent crust pulled off the sphenopalatine region in the first days.
hazards.consequence: Brisk intraoperative bleeding and a classic source of delayed post-op epistaxis.
hazards.prevent: Enlarge the sphenoidotomy superiorly and medially first; coagulate the artery before extending inferiorly (unless a flap is needed). Alternatively, lift the mucosa off the inferior sphenoid face with a Freer and hold it aside while a Kerrison takes the bone. In clinic, leave crust over the sphenopalatine region and over an MT stump alone for at least 10 days ([[p.postoperative-debridement]]).
hazards.recognize: Pulsatile bleed from the inferolateral sphenoidotomy margin; delayed brisk posterior epistaxis; bleeding in clinic as crust is lifted.
hazards.rescue: Suction bipolar at the sphenoid face; return to theatre for delayed bleeding.

hazards.name: Olfactory loss from flap harvest
hazards.site: Upper septum at the olfactory cleft.
hazards.mechanism: Superior incision placed too high removes or cauterises olfactory epithelium.
hazards.consequence: Hyposmia after skull base surgery.
hazards.prevent: Keep the superior incision 1–2 cm below the top of the septum ([[m.nsf-superior-incision]]); use cold instruments or low-power needle cautery there.
hazards.recognize: Post-op smell testing.
hazards.rescue: None effective; olfactory training.

hazards.name: ICA injury at the vidian canal
hazards.site: Posterior end of the vidian canal at the anterior genu of the petrous ICA (foramen lacerum).
hazards.mechanism: Drilling the superolateral circumference of the vidian canal, or drilling blindly posteriorly along it, enters the petrous ICA.
hazards.consequence: Catastrophic haemorrhage, stroke, pseudoaneurysm.
hazards.prevent: Drill only the inferior and medial circumference of the vidian canal (the half below and medial to the nerve), follow the nerve back under vision, and use neuronavigation and Doppler.
hazards.recognize: Sudden high-flow arterial bleeding from the posterior pterygoid base.
hazards.rescue: Two suctions, packing with crushed muscle or a haemostatic, maintain normotension (no induced hypotension; cerebral perfusion matters), then angiography (stent or sacrifice); see [[p.ica-injury-management]].

hazards.name: Internal maxillary artery bleeding in the PPF
hazards.site: Anterior (vascular) layer of the PPF behind the posterior maxillary wall.
hazards.mechanism: Opening the periosteum and dissecting fat bluntly tears the tortuous IMAX or its branches before they are identified.
hazards.consequence: Heavy arterial bleeding that obscures the fossa and can force abandonment. Branches missed during the dissection can go into spasm and bleed profusely after surgery.
hazards.prevent: Open periosteum sharply, identify the IMAX loop and branches, clip or bipolar them before retracting, coagulating every exposed branch even if it is not bleeding; finish the bony window before opening the periosteum; consider preoperative embolisation for vascular tumours.
hazards.recognize: Pulsatile bleeding from the PPF fat.
hazards.rescue: Pressure with a patty, then identify and clip the proximal IMAX; embolisation if uncontrolled.

hazards.name: Maxillary nerve (V2) injury
hazards.site: Upper posterior PPF and foramen rotundum.
hazards.mechanism: Retraction, drilling around the foramen rotundum or dissecting tumour off the nerve.
hazards.consequence: Midface numbness; neuropathic pain.
hazards.prevent: Identify V2 superolaterally early, keep dissection in the plane below it and retract the PPF contents gently laterally as one package.
hazards.recognize: Post-op V2 sensory loss.
hazards.rescue: Supportive; neuropathic pain management.

hazards.name: Dry eye after vidian nerve section
hazards.site: Vidian nerve in its canal or the PPF.
hazards.mechanism: Division of greater superficial petrosal (parasympathetic) fibres to the lacrimal gland. The same deficit follows planned vidian sacrifice in skull base approaches ([[h.vidian-sacrifice-dry-eye]]).
hazards.consequence: Reduced reflex tearing; usually tolerated but can be symptomatic, especially with prior dry eye.
hazards.prevent: Consent for it; prefer posterior nasal neurectomy for rhinorrhoea; assess tear function pre-op. Give artificial tears for the first month.
hazards.recognize: Dry, gritty eye post-op; reduced Schirmer test, which often stays low long term although symptoms usually settle within about a month.
hazards.rescue: Lubricants and ophthalmology follow-up.

hazards.name: Palatal numbness
hazards.site: Greater palatine canal (descending palatine nerves) and the incisive canal (nasopalatine nerve).
hazards.mechanism: Sectioning the descending palatine bundle when taking down the PPF medial wall; dividing the nasopalatine nerve with the NSF anterior incision.
hazards.consequence: Numb palate; usually tolerated and often temporary.
hazards.prevent: Preserve the descending palatine bundle when the exposure allows; counsel.
hazards.recognize: Post-op palatal sensory loss.
hazards.rescue: Reassurance.

hazards.name: DCR ostium closure
hazards.site: Rhinostomy between the opened sac and the lateral nasal wall.
hazards.mechanism: Too small a bony window (sac fundus not exposed above the axilla), sac not fully opened and marsupialised, bare bone left to granulate, or synechia to the MT or septum.
hazards.consequence: Recurrent epiphora and dacryocystitis.
hazards.prevent: Remove bone up to the sac fundus (8–10 mm above the axilla); open the sac fully and lay sac flaps onto nasal mucosal flaps (mucosa-to-mucosa); check that the common canaliculus opening lies in the ostium.
hazards.recognize: Epiphora returns; failed irrigation; closed or granulating ostium on endoscopy.
hazards.rescue: Revision DCR with wider bone removal: most failures come from inadequate exposure of the sac and common canaliculus. Incise new mucosa straight onto bone at the palpated edge of the old osteotomy; a free mucosal graft from the agger nasi can cover bare bone, topical mitomycin C helped in several revision series, and tubes stay longer (4–6 weeks). Address canalicular obstruction separately.

hazards.name: Orbital entry during DCR
hazards.site: Behind the posterior lacrimal crest, where the lacrimal bone meets the lamina papyracea.
hazards.mechanism: Removing bone or sac too far posteriorly; confusing orbital fat with the sac.
hazards.consequence: Orbital fat prolapse, haematoma, medial rectus injury.
hazards.prevent: Stay on the sac; confirm it with light-pipe transillumination or a probe tenting its wall before incising. Take lacrimal bone only up to the uncinate attachment and leave the uncinate: the bone behind it is thin over the orbit.
hazards.recognize: Fat in the field; periorbital bruising.
hazards.rescue: Leave fat alone, avoid packing, monitor vision; manage as orbital haematoma if pressure rises.

hazards.name: Canalicular false passage
hazards.site: Canaliculi and common canaliculus.
hazards.mechanism: Forceful probing or stent passage against resistance.
hazards.consequence: Canalicular stenosis and persistent epiphora despite a patent ostium.
hazards.prevent: Pass probes horizontally with lateral traction on the lid; never force.
hazards.recognize: Probe not tenting the sac medially; bleeding from the punctum.
hazards.rescue: Stent the system and refer to oculoplastics; canalicular obstruction may need a Jones tube.

hazards.name: Parapharyngeal ICA injury during ITF dissection
hazards.site: Behind the cartilaginous Eustachian tube and fossa of Rosenmüller, medial to V3.
hazards.mechanism: Dissection posterior to the ET or lateral to the fossa of Rosenmüller without identifying the ICA; resecting ET cartilage in nasopharyngectomy.
hazards.consequence: Catastrophic haemorrhage; stroke.
hazards.prevent: Use the ET cartilage, the lateral pterygoid plate/V3 and the vidian canal as landmarks; neuronavigation and Doppler; stay anterior to the ET until the ICA is identified.
hazards.recognize: High-flow arterial bleeding deep in the lateral nasopharynx.
hazards.rescue: Packing and pressure, blood-pressure support, urgent angiography; see [[p.ica-injury-management]].

hazards.name: Pterygoid venous plexus bleeding
hazards.site: Infratemporal fossa around the lateral pterygoid muscle, lateral to the PPF.
hazards.mechanism: Entering the ITF or retracting the lateral pterygoid muscle.
hazards.consequence: Persistent venous oozing that fills the field.
hazards.prevent: Reverse Trendelenburg, controlled hypotension, dissect in the fat plane; have haemostatic agents ready.
hazards.recognize: Dark, non-pulsatile welling from the lateral field.
hazards.rescue: Pressure with haemostatic material and patience; bipolar is often ineffective.

principles.name: Mucus goes to the natural ostium
principles.rule: Maxillary mucociliary clearance converges on the natural ostium whatever other openings exist; every antrostomy must include it, and accessory or surgical openings must be joined to it.
principles.why: Messerklinger showed the ciliary pathways are fixed; a separate opening only lets mucus leave and re-enter (recirculation). A patent antrostomy that misses the natural ostium still fails.
principles.caveat: After a large medial maxillectomy gravity and airflow take over, and ostial position matters less.

principles.name: Finish the uncinectomy before looking for the ostium
principles.rule: Remove the uncinate down to the inferior turbinate and up to its superior attachment; if the natural ostium is not visible with a 30°/45° scope, assume uncinate remains.
principles.why: An uncinate remnant hides the natural ostium and is the commonest finding in failed maxillary surgery.

principles.name: Enlarge the antrostomy backwards and downwards
principles.rule: Widen a maxillary antrostomy posteriorly (toward the posterior fontanelle) and inferiorly (toward the IT), not anteriorly (nasolacrimal duct) or superiorly (orbit).
principles.why: The NLD lies a few millimetres in front of the natural ostium and the orbital floor is its roof. Hard bone anteriorly is the lacrimal canal: stop.
principles.caveat: Stop the posterior extension at the posterior wall of the sinus to spare the posterior lateral nasal artery.

principles.name: The maxillary line overlies the lacrimal system
principles.rule: The maxillary line marks the anterior attachment of the uncinate and overlies the lacrimal sac; the nasolacrimal duct lies deep to it or a few millimetres behind it, so uncinectomy and antrostomy must stay well behind the line, not merely behind it.
principles.why: It locates the DCR mucosal incision and the anterior limit for uncinectomy or a mega-antrostomy without CT, even in revision cases where the uncinate is gone. Treating the line as the front edge of the duct invites NLD injury.

principles.name: Examine the nose in three passes
principles.rule: Diagnostic endoscopy is systematic: floor to nasopharynx, then medial to the MT to the sphenoethmoidal recess, then under the MT into the middle meatus, both sides.
principles.why: A fixed sequence finds disease that a targeted look misses (posterior polyps, SER pus, nasopharyngeal lesions) and makes findings comparable over time.

principles.name: The crista ethmoidalis is the SPA sentinel
principles.rule: In SPA ligation, raise the lateral wall flap back to the crista ethmoidalis, remove it, and look behind it for every arterial branch before clipping.
principles.why: The SPF lies immediately behind the crista, and the artery often divides into several branches there; the first vessel seen is rarely the only one.

principles.name: Decide on the nasoseptal flap before you cut the pedicle
principles.rule: In any endonasal case that may need skull base reconstruction, decide on (and if needed raise) the nasoseptal flap, or at least a rescue flap, before sphenoidotomy, posterior septectomy, SPA ligation or transpterygoid work.
principles.why: These steps can divide the posterior septal artery (a sphenoidotomy when it is extended inferiorly); once it is gone the best vascularised reconstructive option is lost on that side.

principles.name: Follow the vidian canal inferomedially to the ICA
principles.rule: The vidian canal leads back to the anterior genu of the petrous ICA; drill its inferior and medial circumference and follow the nerve back under vision.
principles.why: The ICA lies superolateral to the posterior vidian canal at the foramen lacerum, so drilling there is where injury happens.

principles.name: Preserve the L-strut and the keystone
principles.rule: In septoplasty keep at least 10 mm (many advise 15 mm; more if weak) of dorsal and caudal cartilage and never disarticulate the septum from the nasal bones or twist the perpendicular plate.
principles.why: The L-strut holds up the dorsum and tip; twisting the bony septum can fracture the cribriform plate.

principles.name: The lacrimal sac is higher than you think
principles.rule: In endoscopic DCR, expose the whole sac up to its fundus above the MT axilla, open it fully and marsupialise it with mucosa-to-mucosa flaps.
principles.why: Most of the sac lies above the axilla; a low, small rhinostomy leaves a sump and closes.

principles.name: PPF: vessels in front, nerves behind
principles.rule: Enter the PPF from anterior through the periosteum; control and mobilise the IMAX and its branches (anterior vascular layer) before working in the neural layer (V2, PPG, vidian nerve) behind.
principles.why: Blunt dissection through fat before the artery is controlled causes bleeding that ends the operation; the nerves are safe once the vessels are retracted laterally with the fat.

principles.name: Reduce the turbinate, not its mucosa
principles.rule: Treat inferior turbinate hypertrophy by out-fracture and submucosal reduction (bone and/or submucosal tissue), preserving the mucosal surface. Escalate only as needed — out-fracture, then submucosal soft-tissue reduction, then submucosal bone resection — and keep full-thickness resection or aggressive ablation for failures.
principles.why: The mucosa conditions air and gives the sensation of airflow; destroying it risks crusting and empty nose syndrome. Long-term comparative data favour submucosal resection combined with out-fracture, and partial turbinectomy damages the ciliated epithelium more than submucosal radiofrequency reduction.

principles.name: In the ITF, the plate leads to V3 and the tube guards the carotid
principles.rule: Follow the posterior edge of the lateral pterygoid plate up to the foramen ovale and V3; treat the cartilaginous Eustachian tube as the anterior marker of the parapharyngeal ICA, which lies posterolateral to it.
principles.why: These are fixed bony and cartilaginous guides when tumour distorts soft tissue, and they define where endonasal lateral dissection must stop until the ICA is identified.

principles.name: Canine fossa puncture at the crosshair
principles.rule: Place a canine fossa trephine where the mid-pupillary line crosses a horizontal line through the nasal floor.
principles.why: This avoids most anterior superior alveolar nerve branches and the infraorbital foramen, lowering dental numbness and facial pain.

principles.name: Make the field dry before the first cut
principles.rule: Place decongestant pledgets accurately — high enough to shrink the septal and turbinate swell bodies and open the middle meatus, not just on the floor — infiltrate lidocaine with adrenaline where you will incise, and give both time to work (at least 5 minutes for topical decongestion, up to about 15 minutes for infiltration) before the first incision.
principles.why: Endoscopic surgery depends on a clear view, and bleeding is what takes it away. Heart rate and blood pressure often peak in the first quarter-hour after induction; operating before vasoconstriction has taken effect means more mucosal trauma and bleeding, especially at the anterior septum, the MT head and the lateral wall, and badly placed pledgets leave the middle meatus and frontal recess hidden. Total intravenous anaesthesia reduced blood loss compared with inhalational anaesthesia in a systematic review.
principles.caveat: Local vasoconstriction does not control a named artery: for heavy bleeding from the SPA territory use a transpalatal greater palatine injection with a depth-limited needle ([[m.greater-palatine-canal-length]]) or control the artery ([[p.spa-ligation]]).

principles.name: Climb the maxillary access ladder one rung at a time
principles.rule: Choose the least extensive endonasal route that reaches the lesion's attachment: middle meatal antrostomy, mega-antrostomy, modified (turbinate- and duct-sparing) medial maxillectomy, total medial maxillectomy with or without the nasolacrimal duct, transseptal (cross-court) routes, and finally the endoscopic Denker approach ([[p.endoscopic-denker]]) — before an open approach.
principles.why: Each rung buys more anterolateral reach at the price of more morbidity (duct, turbinate, infraorbital and alveolar nerves, alar support). Cadaver studies put numbers on the steps (small single series, angles of instrument reach as reported in atlas chapters): total over modified medial maxillectomy about 12°; medial maxillectomy over antrostomy about 18.5°, and a 1 cm Denker maxillotomy about 33.5° more; a cross-court window about 15° over an ipsilateral approach, raising access lateral to the infraorbital nerve from 63% to 98% of specimens and to the anterior wall from 25% to 95%; septal dislocation about 20° over total medial maxillectomy.
principles.caveat: The ladder is a guide, not a rule: surgeon preference, tumour extent and margins, sinus geometry and whether a DCR is acceptable all shift the choice. A cross-court window needs an unscarred septum and angled instruments; septal dislocation (cartilage freed from the crest and the bony septum and swung across) allows straight instruments and four hands through one nostril but is limited by a concave anterior maxilla or a prominent opposite piriform rim; a limited septal window made for access can later serve as the transseptal route. The prelacrimal approach ([[p.prelacrimal-approach]]) reaches the anterior and lateral antrum while keeping the IT and duct when the recess is wide enough. Canine fossa trephination adds no reach for a tumour on the anterior wall.

procedures.name: Diagnostic nasal endoscopy (three-pass)
indications: Chronic rhinosinusitis diagnosis and staging
Unilateral symptoms, epistaxis, anosmia or suspected tumour
Post-operative surveillance
Unilateral otitis media with effusion in an adult (exclude nasopharyngeal carcinoma)
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, both sides, 0° (or 30°) rigid endoscope after topical decongestant and anaesthetic.

steps.do: Decongest and anaesthetise both sides; inspect the vestibule, valve and anterior septum.
steps.think: Is the valve or an anterior deviation the real obstruction? Note bleeding points on the anterior septum.

steps.do: First pass: along the floor medial to the IT to the choana; inspect the nasopharynx, both ET orifices and fossae of Rosenmüller.
steps.think: Any asymmetry or mass in the fossa of Rosenmüller means biopsy under endoscopic control; a pulsatile bulge means imaging first.

steps.do: Second pass: between MT and septum to the posterior nasal cavity; inspect the superior turbinate, SER and sphenoid ostium.
steps.think: Pus in the SER means posterior group disease (posterior ethmoid or sphenoid). Look up into the olfactory cleft on the way back.

steps.do: Third pass: under the MT head into the middle meatus; inspect the uncinate, hiatus, bulla and any accessory ostium.
steps.think: Pus or polyps from the hiatus mean anterior group disease; an accessory ostium seen here is not the natural ostium.

steps.do: Repeat on the other side; record findings with a validated score (e.g. Lund–Kennedy) and take cultures from pus under vision.
steps.think: Findings must be comparable at the next visit; unilateral disease prompts the question of tumour, fungus or dental source.

procedures.endpoints: Both sides seen in three passes, including both fossae of Rosenmüller, the SER and the middle meatus; findings scored and recorded.
pitfalls: Skipping the nasopharynx in a patient with unilateral OME
Calling an accessory ostium the natural ostium
Scope trauma to the septum or MT causing bleeding that ends the exam

procedures.name: Endoscopic septoplasty
indications: Symptomatic nasal obstruction from septal deviation
Access for sinus or skull base surgery
Contact-point headache with a matching deviation (selected)
Septal spur causing epistaxis or crusting
Deviation narrowing the middle meatus in recurrent or chronic rhinosinusitis (with sinus surgery)
Nasal obstruction in selected patients with obstructive sleep apnoea
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, 0° endoscope, hemitransfixion or Killian incision on the side of the most anterior deviation, or, for an isolated spur, a targeted incision in front of it or a horizontal incision along the spur's apex with flaps raised above and below it and simply redraped once the spur is removed (directed septoplasty).

preop.check: Locate the deviation (valve vs posterior, cartilage vs bone) and classify it ([[c.mladina-septal]]).
preop.why: Valve deviations explain obstruction; posterior deviations mainly limit access, so a limited endoscopic resection may be enough.

preop.check: Base the diagnosis on examination; CT is not needed to diagnose a septal deviation.
preop.why: CT can understate the deviation seen clinically; when one exists, use it for posterior deflections and a concha bullosa that anterior rhinoscopy misses.

preop.check: Check skull base integrity and the perpendicular plate on CT when available.
preop.why: The perpendicular plate is fused to the cribriform plate; a thin or dehiscent skull base increases CSF leak risk.

preop.check: Assess dorsal and tip support and prior surgery.
preop.why: Weak or previously resected cartilage leaves little L-strut to spare.

steps.do: After topical decongestion, infiltrate lidocaine with adrenaline under the mucoperichondrium and give it time to work (about 15 minutes for full effect, [[pr.dry-field-before-first-cut]]); make the incision and raise the mucoperichondrial flap in the subperichondrial plane.
steps.think: Blue-grey cartilage and a bloodless plane confirm the right depth; white cartilage with bleeding means you are too superficial.

steps.do: Extend posteriorly over the bony-cartilaginous junction onto the perpendicular plate and vomer; raise an inferior tunnel from the floor and join it to the anterior tunnel over the maxillary crest.
steps.think: Mucosa over a spur tears: approach the spur from above and below, not from its crest.

steps.do: Disarticulate the cartilage from the bone at the bony-cartilaginous junction and raise the contralateral flap on the bony septum.
steps.think: Only one side of cartilage is elevated where possible so the cartilage keeps a blood supply on the other side.

steps.do: Resect or straighten the deviated cartilage and bone, preserving the L-strut; cut the perpendicular plate with through-cutting forceps and remove spurs with a chisel.
steps.think: How much dorsal and caudal strut is left? At least 10 mm (15 mm by some authors, [[m.l-strut-width]]), more if thin. The posterior bony septum carries no support and need not be kept — but cut it, never twist bone near the skull base.

steps.do: Caudal deviation: score the concave face of the caudal cartilage vertically to weaken its memory and free it from the maxillary crest; then either trim the strip lying in the crest groove, swing the septum to the midline and suture it to the nasal spine (swinging door), or, without trimming, set its base on the far side of the crest from the obstruction (doorstop).
steps.think: Scoring and freeing weaken the caudal strut, so fix it securely. A deformity beyond this needs an ethmoid-bone batten ("sandwich") graft, which can be placed endonasally, or an open extracorporeal septoplasty (septum removed, rebuilt as an L-strut and replaced).

steps.do: Replace straightened cartilage between the flaps where support or a perforation risk exists; repair tears; quilt the flaps and/or place splints.
steps.think: Are there opposing tears? Close one side and interpose cartilage.

steps.do: Postoperative: remove splints after 2–7 days. Some surgeons give an anti-staphylococcal antibiotic while packing or splints are in place to prevent toxic shock syndrome; practice varies.

procedures.endpoints: Septum in the midline from valve to choana with a clear corridor for the scope; intact L-strut of at least 10–15 mm ([[m.l-strut-width]]); flaps apposed without opposing tears.
pitfalls: Under-correcting the caudal septum and valve area
Twisting the perpendicular plate
Over-resection of the dorsal strut
Unrecognised septal haematoma

procedures.name: Inferior turbinate reduction
indications: Nasal obstruction from inferior turbinate hypertrophy (allergic or non-allergic chronic rhinitis) not responding to medical therapy
Compensatory hypertrophy opposite a septal deviation
Access for inferior meatal or skull base work
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, 0° endoscope.

preop.check: Decongestion test: mucosal (shrinks) vs bony hypertrophy. Imaging is not needed for the inferior turbinate itself.
preop.why: Mucosal hypertrophy responds to submucosal energy techniques; bony hypertrophy needs out-fracture or submucosal bone resection. A sinus CT, when one exists, also shows the bone.

steps.do: Out-fracture: medialise the IT with a Freer, then press it inferolaterally along its whole length — its bony attachment is angled, so pushing straight laterally moves it poorly.
steps.think: Does it stay lateral? If it springs back, bony hypertrophy needs submucosal bone reduction. Be gentle toward the inferior meatus: the nasolacrimal duct opens under the anterior IT.

steps.do: Submucosal reduction: incise the head, raise a medial mucoperiosteal flap and reduce the bone and/or submucosal tissue (microdebrider, coblation or radiofrequency), keeping the medial mucosa intact.
steps.think: Remove volume, not surface; the anterior head at the valve — roughly its first 2 cm — gives most of the airway benefit.

steps.do: Check the posterior end and coagulate any bleeding at the tail under vision.
steps.think: Tail bleeding is arterial (IT branch of the posterior lateral nasal artery); control it now rather than pack.

procedures.endpoints: Reduced, lateralised turbinate with intact medial mucosa and an open valve and inferior airway; no bleeding at the tail.
pitfalls: Resecting mucosa (crusting, empty nose)
Missing the head at the valve
Leaving posterior bleeding
Aggressive thermal reduction (mucosal slough and prolonged crusting)
Full-thickness resection of the anterior end: bare bone, slow healing and heavy crusting

procedures.name: Uncinectomy (standard and swing-door)
indications: First step of FESS for maxillary, anterior ethmoid or frontal disease
Access to the maxillary natural ostium
Access to the lacrimal sac region (with DCR) and frontal recess
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, middle meatus, 0° then 30°/45° endoscope.

preop.check: Uncinate position and superior attachment on coronal and sagittal CT ([[c.uncinate-superior-attachment]]).
preop.why: Tells you whether the frontal sinus drains medial or lateral to it and what the top of the uncinate is attached to.

preop.check: Is the uncinate lateralised on the orbit (atelectasis, hypoplasia)?
preop.why: Then the lamina papyracea lies immediately behind it: use a retrograde technique and cut medially.

preop.check: Haller cell, accessory ostium and infraorbital canal.
preop.why: Structures that narrow the infundibulum or change where the ostium is.

steps.do: Medialise the MT gently; identify the uncinate behind the maxillary line and palpate its free edge with a ball probe in the hiatus semilunaris.
steps.think: Does the probe pass behind the uncinate freely? A lateralised uncinate is already on the orbit.

steps.do: Standard: incise the uncinate from its superior attachment down to the IT with a sickle knife or Freer, cutting parallel to the orbit. Swing-door: with a ball probe behind its free edge, fracture the uncinate forward and medially at its lateral-wall attachment, then cut its superior and inferior attachments.
steps.think: Instrument tips point medially, never laterally; the swing-door avoids a knife aimed at the orbit.

steps.do: Remove the horizontal (inferior) part with a back-biter down to the IT and trim the remnant with a through-cutter or microdebrider.
steps.think: Back-bite only a couple of bites: hard bone anteriorly is the nasolacrimal canal.

steps.do: Remove the vertical (superior) part up to its attachment with a 45° through-cutter under a 30°/45° scope.
steps.think: What is the top attached to? Cut, never pull, if it goes to the skull base or MT.

steps.do: Inspect the infundibulum with a 30°/45° scope and identify the maxillary natural ostium.
steps.think: If the natural ostium is not seen, uncinate remains. Do not enlarge anything until it is.

procedures.endpoints: No uncinate remnant from IT to superior attachment; natural ostium visible; lamina papyracea intact.
pitfalls: Uncinate remnant hiding the natural ostium
Orbital entry with a sickle knife in a lateralised uncinate
Twisting the superior attachment (skull base, MT)

procedures.name: Middle meatal maxillary antrostomy
indications: Chronic or recurrent acute maxillary sinusitis failing medical therapy
Fungal ball, antrochoanal polyp, mucocele
Access for biopsy or wider maxillary procedures
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, middle meatus, 0° and 30°/45° endoscopes; 70° to inspect the antrum.

preop.check: Natural ostium, infundibulum and accessory ostia.
preop.why: The antrostomy must include the natural ostium.

preop.check: Nasolacrimal canal position relative to the ostium.
preop.why: Sets the anterior limit.

preop.check: Orbital floor, infraorbital canal type and Haller cell.
preop.why: Sets the superior limit and flags nerve risk.

preop.check: Dental source (periapical lucency, oroantral fistula).
preop.why: Odontogenic disease needs dental treatment as well.

steps.do: Complete the uncinectomy and identify the natural ostium ([[p.uncinectomy]]).
steps.think: No enlargement before the natural ostium is seen.

steps.do: Enlarge the ostium posteriorly into the posterior fontanelle with side-biting or through-cutting forceps or a microdebrider, and inferiorly toward the IT.
steps.think: Backwards and downwards; the orbit is above and the NLD is a few mm in front.

steps.do: Join any accessory ostium to the antrostomy.
steps.think: One opening, not two: separate openings recirculate mucus.

steps.do: Inspect the antrum with 30°/45°/70° scopes; remove disease (fungal debris, polyps, and every trace of allergic mucin — 70° scope and saline irrigation) with curved suction and instruments while preserving mucosa.
steps.think: Where is the infraorbital nerve? Keep debriders off the roof. Disease in the anterior or alveolar recess may need a canine fossa or prelacrimal route. Allergic mucin left behind keeps the mucosa oedematous.

steps.do: Check the MT is stable and not lateralising; consider a spacer or medialisation.
steps.think: An unstable MT will scar across the antrostomy.

procedures.endpoints: Single antrostomy including the natural ostium, sized to the disease — minimal enlargement of the natural ostium for recurrent acute sinusitis with non-polypoid mucosa, typically 1–2 cm for CRS, and wide (full uncinate and fontanelle removal back to the palatine bone) for polyposis, hyperplastic mucosa, fungus, revision or topical-therapy access; NLD, orbit and posterior lateral nasal artery intact; MT stable.
pitfalls: Antrostomy separate from the natural ostium
Anterior extension into the NLD
Stripping antral mucosa
Missing disease in the anterior/alveolar recess

procedures.name: Endoscopic (modified) medial maxillectomy
indications: Inverted papilloma or benign tumour attached to the maxillary walls

Recalcitrant maxillary sinusitis after failed antrostomy (mega-antrostomy), e.g. cystic fibrosis, extensive allergic mucin, prolapsed orbital fat after medial orbital decompression, or a scarred sinus after mucosal stripping (Caldwell-Luc)
Access to the anterior, lateral and inferior antrum, PPF and ITF
Selected malignancy with clear margins
procedures.corridor: Transnasal; modified (turbinate-sparing) variants keep the IT head and NLD, full variants remove the medial wall with the IT and divide the NLD.

preop.check: Tumour attachment site (focal hyperostosis on CT, MRI to separate tumour from retained secretions).
preop.why: Decides the extent: resect the attachment with its underlying bone.

preop.check: NLD position and prelacrimal recess width ([[c.prelacrimal-recess]]).
preop.why: Decides whether to preserve, displace or divide the NLD.

preop.check: Posterior wall, PPF and orbital floor integrity.
preop.why: Erosion changes the plan and the risk to IMAX and the orbit.

preop.check: Plan vascular control: a transpalatal greater palatine injection (needle bent to limit depth, [[m.greater-palatine-canal-length]]) or a transnasal injection over the crista ethmoidalis just below the MT's posterior attachment (needle bent about 1 cm).
preop.why: Vasoconstriction in the PPF and SPA territory reduces bleeding during wall removal ([[pr.dry-field-before-first-cut]]).

preop.check: Septal deviation blocking the middle meatus.
preop.why: A limited septal window may be enough, and it can later serve as a transseptal route to the anterolateral antrum ([[pr.maxillary-access-ladder]]).

steps.do: Wide middle meatal antrostomy including the natural ostium.
steps.think: Map the tumour attachment before removing landmarks.

steps.do: Raise a medially based nasal floor mucosal flap before any bone cuts: anterior cut just below the IT attachment and slightly behind the valve of Hasner, posterior cut at the level of the posterior maxillary wall, joined by a cut placed as close to the IT attachment as possible for length; park it on the floor or drape it over the septum.
steps.think: This flap goes back over the bare bony ridge at the end: less crusting and contracture.

steps.do: Cut the IT: clamp it with a haemostat for at least 30 seconds at the junction of its anterior third and posterior two-thirds, cut along the crushed line from just behind the nasolacrimal duct back to the posterior maxillary wall and medial pterygoid plate, and remove the posterior two-thirds, keeping the head (modified technique) — or detach the whole IT for more room. Carry cuts down the medial wall to the nasal floor.
steps.think: How far forward must you go? If only the posterior wall and floor are involved, preserve the IT head and NLD. Most of the antrum lies below the IT's upper attachment, so removing its posterior two-thirds opens the sinus floor; keeping the head preserves normal nasal airflow.

steps.do: Mark the anterior osteotomy by puncturing the medial wall with a J-curette just behind and below the valve of Hasner; run the inferior cut back through the posterior fontanelle with through-cutting forceps, then forward with a backbiter toward the anterior wall.
steps.think: Staying behind Hasner's valve keeps the duct in the modified operation; divide it only if the anterior wall must be reached (next step).

steps.do: Identify the nasolacrimal duct in its canal; drill it out and divide it sharply and obliquely if the anterior wall must be reached, or preserve it.
steps.think: Divide sharply high in the canal and consider marsupialising: crushed ducts stenose.

steps.do: Remove the medial wall back to the palatine bone, controlling posterior lateral nasal branches and the SPA if needed.
steps.think: Control the SPA before removing the posterior medial wall.

steps.do: Resect the tumour and strip the mucosa at the attachment; drill the underlying bone (hyperostosis).
steps.think: Drilling the attachment reduces recurrence; watch the infraorbital canal on the roof.

steps.do: Drill any residual inferior ridge of the medial wall flush with the nasal floor (diamond bur) — in a contracted or hypoplastic sinus only down to its floor — lay the floor flap back over the bare bone, and check haemostasis and the orbit.
steps.think: A flat transition lets the cavity self-clean and be examined in clinic.

steps.do: Postoperative: hold the floor flap down with a small spacer or dissolvable packing against the IT remnant until the first visit, and leave the posterior IT stump alone for about 2 weeks.
steps.think: Debriding the stump while its clot dissolves invites a bleed. Expect heavier crusting than after an antrostomy, as after a Draf III: book more frequent clinic debridement ([[p.postoperative-debridement]]).

procedures.endpoints: Attachment site cleared and drilled; one common cavity of nose and antrum with a smooth floor; NLD preserved or cleanly divided; orbit, ION and IMAX intact.
pitfalls: Leaving anterior-wall attachment unreachable without prelacrimal, canine fossa or Denker ([[p.endoscopic-denker]]) extension
Crushing the NLD
Crusting from removal of the whole IT
Stripping antral mucosa when operating for inflammatory disease (inflammation, poor clearance, contracture)
With prolapsed orbital fat, making the upper cuts first: make the inferior and anterior cuts first to see where fat fills the infundibulum, then fold the wall away from the fat

procedures.name: Prelacrimal recess approach to the maxillary sinus
indications: Disease of the anterior, lateral (zygomatic) or inferior antrum: inverted papilloma, fungal ball, cysts, foreign body
Access to the PPF/ITF while preserving the IT and NLD
procedures.corridor: Transnasal: a curved incision on the lateral wall in front of the IT head, a mucosal flap with the IT, and removal of bone in front of the NLD to enter the antrum through the prelacrimal recess.

preop.check: Width of the prelacrimal recess on axial CT ([[c.prelacrimal-recess]]).
preop.why: Narrow recesses (Type I) need extensive anterior bone removal and NLD displacement.

preop.check: Site of disease and relation to the anterior wall and ION.
preop.why: Confirms the approach reaches it and flags the nerve.

steps.do: Incise vertically in front of the IT head along the piriform aperture and down to the nasal floor; raise the mucoperiosteum with the IT and inferior meatus mucosa.
steps.think: Stay subperiosteal; the flap will be replaced at the end.

steps.do: Remove the bone of the frontal process of the maxilla/anterior medial wall in front of the nasolacrimal canal with a chisel or drill to open the prelacrimal recess.
steps.think: Expose, do not breach, the bony NLD canal; displace the IT–NLD complex medially as a unit.

steps.do: Enter the antrum and work with 0°–70° scopes on the anterior, lateral and inferior walls.
steps.think: Keep off the roof ridge and the anterior superior alveolar nerve in the anterior wall.

steps.do: Open the natural ostium from inside if needed; replace the IT–NLD flap and suture the incision.
steps.think: Restores normal anatomy and drainage.

procedures.endpoints: Disease removed from the anterior/lateral/inferior antrum with IT and NLD preserved and the flap replaced.
pitfalls: Type I recess forcing NLD injury
Dental numbness from anterior bone removal

procedures.name: Canine fossa trephination and Caldwell-Luc
indications: Anterior or lateral antral disease unreachable through a middle meatal antrostomy (trephine as an adjunct port), e.g. severe maxillary polyposis
Caldwell-Luc (sublabial antrostomy) now rarely: foreign bodies, some cysts or tumours, when endoscopic routes fail
procedures.corridor: Sublabial/transfacial: trocar puncture of the canine fossa (trephine) or a sublabial incision with an anterior wall window (Caldwell-Luc).

preop.check: Maxillary sinus size, anterior wall thickness and dentition.
preop.why: Hypoplastic sinuses and unerupted teeth (children) are contraindications.

steps.do: Mark the puncture at the intersection of the mid-pupillary line and a horizontal line through the nasal floor.
steps.think: This crosshair avoids most ASA nerve branches and stays below the infraorbital foramen.

steps.do: Trephine: pass the trocar through the gingivobuccal sulcus and anterior wall into the antrum; introduce a scope or microdebrider through the port while viewing via the antrostomy.
steps.think: Two-port work: view from one port, instrument from the other.

steps.do: Caldwell-Luc: sublabial incision above the gingival sulcus, subperiosteal elevation, anterior wall window in the canine fossa preserving the infraorbital nerve, then remove disease and ensure middle meatal drainage.
steps.think: Keep the window small and the incision high; drainage must be through the natural ostium, not an inferior meatal window.

steps.do: Close the sublabial wound in layers.
steps.think: Protects against oroantral fistula.

procedures.endpoints: Disease cleared from the anterior and lateral antrum with a functioning middle meatal antrostomy; no oroantral communication.
pitfalls: Medial or high puncture (dental numbness, ION injury)
Stripping all antral mucosa
Inferior meatal drainage instead of the natural ostium
Trephining for a tumour attached to the anterior wall: no added reach, and the port can pass through the tumour — use a prelacrimal or Denker route ([[pr.maxillary-access-ladder]])

procedures.name: Endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy
indications: Primary acquired nasolacrimal duct obstruction (epiphora, dacryocystitis)
Post-traumatic or post-surgical NLD obstruction
Mucocele of the lacrimal sac
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, 0° (and 30°) endoscope, lateral wall at the MT axilla.

preop.check: Level of obstruction by syringing/probing (canalicular vs sac/duct); dacryocystography and lacrimal scintigraphy when the level is unclear or a functional block is suspected.
