preop.why: DCR fixes a post-sac obstruction; canalicular obstruction needs a different operation. Imaging can also reveal a tight common canaliculus that will keep the eye watering after a DCR.

preop.check: Septal deviation, MT and agger nasi on CT or endoscopy.
preop.why: May need septoplasty or MT/agger work for access. If a septoplasty is needed, incise on the side opposite the DCR: the endoscope will not tear that flap, less blood runs onto the lens, and septum-to-lateral-wall synechiae are less likely.

preop.check: Suspicion of tumour (bloody tears, mass).
preop.why: Biopsy the sac.

steps.do: After decongestion, infiltrate the MT axilla and the mucosa over the frontal process with lidocaine and adrenaline; raise a posteriorly based mucosal flap on the lateral wall above and in front of the MT axilla, over the maxillary line and frontal process.
steps.think: Flap starts about 8–10 mm above the axilla to reach the fundus.

steps.do: Remove the frontal process of the maxilla with a punch (Hajek–Koffler or Kerrison) for as long as it will bite, then a DCR bur; flake off the lacrimal bone up to, but not including, the uncinate attachment, exposing the whole sac up to its fundus.
steps.think: Is the fundus exposed? Most of the sac lies above the axilla. Open the punch after each bite so any caught sac slips free instead of tearing, and keep the bur at the bone–sac interface, never between sac and bone. Leave the uncinate: the bone behind it is thin and the orbit lies there.

steps.do: Pass a lacrimal probe through the canaliculus to tent the medial sac wall; incise the sac vertically and open it with relaxing cuts into anterior and posterior flaps.
steps.think: Probe tenting confirms sac, not orbit; never force the probe.

steps.do: Marsupialise: lay the sac flaps onto the trimmed nasal mucosal flaps and, where exposed, onto agger nasi mucosa (mucosa to mucosa); check the common canaliculus opening lies within the ostium; pass silicone tubes through the puncta when the common canaliculus is narrow.
steps.think: No bare bone, flat sac: apposed mucosa heals by primary intention and keeps the ostium open. Tubes dilate a narrow common canaliculus, help seat the flaps (gelatin sponge slid down them) and draw tears by capillarity.

steps.do: Postoperative: remove the tubes at about 4 weeks and confirm patency with the fluorescein dye disappearance test and a Valsalva bubble test at the ostium.

procedures.endpoints: Sac fully opened and flat on the lateral wall from fundus to duct, common canaliculus draining into the ostium, mucosal edges apposed; fluorescein or saline passes freely.
pitfalls: Low, small rhinostomy below the fundus
Bare bone and granulation
Unrecognised canalicular obstruction
Synechia to the MT

procedures.name: Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation
indications: Posterior epistaxis (bleeding that adequate anterior packing does not control) failing or recurring after posterior packing or cautery
Early alternative to posterior packing and admission within a structured epistaxis pathway (shorter stay, lower cost and less morbidity than packing-first care)
Recurrent posterior epistaxis
Adjunct to control bleeding before posterior nasal or skull base surgery
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, posterior middle meatus, 0°/30° endoscope; medial maxillary wall and palatine bone.

preop.check: Where is the bleeding? Anterior septum, posterior lateral wall or superior (AEA territory).
preop.why: Superior bleeding may need AEA ligation as well.

preop.check: Coagulopathy, anticoagulants, hypertension, HHT.
preop.why: Correct what can be corrected. Bleeding driven by anticoagulants or antiplatelets is better managed with limited cautery and resorbable packing than with ligation, and in HHT ligation rarely gives lasting control ([[dz.hht]]).

preop.check: Septal deviation limiting access.
preop.why: May need a limited septoplasty.

steps.do: Get room and a workable field: medialise the MT gently with a Freer, pledget the middle meatus and remove a large uncinate if it blocks the view; if bleeding still obscures, slow it with a transpalatal greater palatine injection of lidocaine with adrenaline ([[m.greater-palatine-canal-length]]), warm (about 50 °C) irrigation, decongestant pledgets or bipolar. Optionally make a small maxillary antrostomy to identify the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus as a landmark.
steps.think: The SPF lies just behind the posterior wall of the antrum at the MT tail.

steps.do: Incise the lateral wall mucosa vertically about 1 cm anterior to the MT posterior attachment and raise a posteriorly based subperiosteal flap.
steps.think: Stay on bone: the flap brings the vessels with it.

steps.do: Identify the crista ethmoidalis and remove it; find the SPA branches emerging behind it.
steps.think: How many branches? Expect two or more; look behind and below the crista.

steps.do: Clip and/or bipolar every branch, including the posterior lateral nasal artery and posterior septal branch; follow toward the sphenoid face if needed.
steps.think: Missing the posterior septal branch is the classic cause of failure. The posterior nasal nerves (including the nasopalatine) leave the foramen with the vessels; dividing them causes no recognised deficit, but they can often be teased off before clipping.

steps.do: Replace the flap; inspect for other bleeding sites.
steps.think: Ongoing superior bleeding points to the AEA.

procedures.endpoints: All SPA branches behind the crista controlled, including the posterior septal branch; no active bleeding.
pitfalls: Clipping one branch only
Missing an accessory foramen
Forgetting the AEA source

procedures.name: Endoscopic posterior nasal neurectomy
indications: Intractable rhinorrhoea in allergic or non-allergic (vasomotor) rhinitis failing medical therapy
Often combined with inferior turbinate reduction
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, posterior middle meatus at the SPF (same exposure as SPA ligation), 0°/30° endoscope.

preop.check: Confirm that rhinorrhoea, not obstruction alone, is the target symptom.
preop.why: The operation reduces secretion; obstruction needs turbinate or septal surgery.

preop.check: SPF position and septal access on CT.
preop.why: Plans the flap and the approach.

steps.do: Raise a posteriorly based lateral wall flap to the crista ethmoidalis as for SPA ligation.
steps.think: Same landmarks as SPA ligation.

steps.do: Identify the posterior nasal nerve bundle emerging from the SPF with the SPA; separate nerve from artery.
steps.think: Preserve the artery where possible (pedicle for any future flap); small accessory nerve branches emerge nearby.

steps.do: Divide or cauterise the nerve bundle (and small accessory branches); replace the flap.
steps.think: Complete section of all branches determines the effect.

procedures.endpoints: Posterior nasal nerve bundle divided at the SPF with the SPA preserved or controlled.
pitfalls: Arterial injury causing bleeding
Incomplete section of accessory branches

procedures.name: Endoscopic vidian neurectomy
indications: Intractable vasomotor or allergic rhinorrhoea after failure of medical therapy and less invasive procedures (largely replaced by posterior nasal neurectomy)
Part of the transpterygoid approach (vidian nerve sectioned for exposure)
procedures.corridor: Transnasal: transmaxillary/trans-SPF to the anterior opening of the vidian canal in the posterior PPF, or transsphenoidal to a vidian ridge in the sphenoid floor.

preop.check: Vidian canal course and relation to the sphenoid floor on coronal CT ([[c.vidian-canal-type]]).
preop.why: A canal above or on the floor (types 1–2, [[v.vidian-canal-protrusion]]) can be reached from inside the sphenoid; an embedded type 3 canal is reached through the PPF.

preop.check: Tear function and dry eye history.
preop.why: Section reduces reflex tearing.

steps.do: Expose the SPF (flap to the crista), control the SPA and remove the medial PPF wall (palatine perpendicular plate) as needed.
steps.think: Control vessels before looking for the nerve.

steps.do: Retract the PPF contents laterally and find the vidian canal opening at the pterygoid base, inferomedial to foramen rotundum; distinguish it from the smaller, more medial palatovaginal canal and its pharyngeal nerve.
steps.think: The palatovaginal canal is medial and smaller; the vidian nerve enters the PPG. The vidian and pharyngeal nerves together tether the fossa contents: dividing both lets them move laterally.

steps.do: Divide the vidian nerve (and the pharyngeal nerve) at the canal openings with a sickle knife and coagulate the vidian artery; inspect the whole bony rim of the canal to confirm a complete cut, then plug the canal with bone wax. Do not drill posteriorly along the canal.
steps.think: Posteriorly the canal leads to the ICA genu: neurectomy needs no deep drilling. Relapse at 12–24 months is put down to nerve regrowth; a complete cut and a wax plug reduce it.

procedures.endpoints: Vidian nerve divided at the anterior canal with the whole rim checked and the canal plugged, haemostasis, and no posterior drilling.
pitfalls: Confusing the palatovaginal canal with the vidian canal
Posterior drilling toward the ICA
Unwarned dry eye
Incomplete section or an unplugged canal (relapse from reinnervation at 12–24 months)

procedures.name: Nasoseptal flap harvest (including rescue flap)
indications: Reconstruction of skull base defects after expanded endonasal approaches, especially with high-flow CSF leaks
Large anterior skull base or clival defects
Rescue flap: preserving the pedicle in pituitary or other cases where a flap may prove necessary

Medial orbital wall reconstruction after extensive endoscopic dissection of a mid or anterior orbital lesion ([[p.orbital-tumor-resection]]), to limit enophthalmos and diplopia from lost orbital volume

Mini flap — as little as 5–10 mm of posterior septal mucosa on the pedicle — to cover bare bone at the lower rim of a sphenoid drill-out for recalcitrant chronic sphenoiditis ([[p.sphenoid-drill-out]])
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, 0° endoscope; mucoperichondrium/mucoperiosteum of one side of the septum pedicled on the posterior septal artery between the sphenoid ostium and the choana.

preop.check: Septal integrity: prior septoplasty, perforation, deviation and spurs.
preop.why: Previous surgery or a perforation may make the flap unusable on that side.

preop.check: Expected defect size and site.
preop.why: Sets the design, a ladder of three sizes: a short flap, its anterior cut at about the head of the MT, for sellar and planum defects; a full-length flap taking the whole septal mucoperichondrium (the donor septum then resurfaced from the other side) for ethmoid, cribriform or clival defects; and an extended flap onto the nasal floor and inferior meatus for the largest. One flap covers two neighboring zones, not three ([[pr.one-flap-two-regions]]).

preop.check: Which side to harvest.
preop.why: Take the side opposite a transpterygoid/PPF approach, or the side with the better septum; tumour involving the septum or pedicle excludes it. For clival tumors, harvest opposite the tumor's most lateral extension and park the flap in a wide maxillary antrostomy, clear of the clival corridor ([[p.transclival-approach]]).

preop.check: Age under about 14 years.
preop.why: The septum is short relative to the skull base in children, so the flap may not reach the defect; plan an alternative ([[p.skull-base-reconstruction]]).

steps.do: Identify the sphenoid ostium and choana and the pedicle between them; lateralise the MT and IT for room.
steps.think: Decide flap vs rescue flap now, before any sphenoidotomy or septectomy.

steps.do: Superior incision: along the septum 1–2 cm below the top of the septum, starting at the inferior margin of the sphenoid ostium and running forward.
steps.think: Spare the olfactory strip ([[m.nsf-superior-incision]]); use cold steel or low-power needle cautery.

steps.do: Inferior incision: down the posterior free edge of the septum along the choanal arch and vomer to the hard palate, then forward along the junction of septum and nasal floor — or, for extra width, laterally across the floor along the posterior edge of the hard palate (parallel to the hard–soft palate junction) to the inferior meatus, and forward from there.
steps.think: Width comes from the floor: extend laterally for large defects.

steps.do: Anterior vertical incision joining the two, placed according to the length needed (up to the mucocutaneous junction for maximum length).
steps.think: Longer flap reaches further (anterior skull base, clivus) but leaves more donor site.

steps.do: Elevate subperichondrially/subperiosteally from anterior to posterior, preserving the pedicle; park the flap in the nasopharynx or maxillary sinus until reconstruction.
steps.think: Do not tear the flap over the bony-cartilaginous junction or spurs. Tears are most frequent where the mucoperichondrial fibres cross over the maxillary crest near the nasal spine: free them from the floor upward, joining the floor tunnel to the septal tunnel, rather than pulling down from above.

steps.do: Rescue flap alternative: make only the superior incision and elevate the posterior part of the pedicle off the sphenoid face, leaving the septum intact so that the full flap can be completed later if needed.
steps.think: Protects the pedicle during a wide sphenoidotomy without committing the whole septum. When instruments must cross from the other nostril, cut a small mucosal window beside the sphenoid ostium on that side too, its lower incision parallel to the ostium, so that side's pedicle also survives ([[p.transsellar-approach]]).

steps.do: At reconstruction, lay the flap with its raw (perichondrial/periosteal) surface against the defect and denuded bone margins and its mucosa facing the nasal cavity; ensure bony contact all round and no mucosa left under the flap.
steps.think: Is the pedicle kinked or stretched? Is all mucosa removed from the defect edges?

steps.do: Cover the donor site (reverse flap from the other side, free graft or healing by secondary intention) and splint the septum with thin silicone sheets for at least 3 weeks.
steps.think: Bare septum crusts until it remucosalizes, usually by about 3 months; covering and splinting speed healing.

procedures.endpoints: Flap of sufficient size elevated on an intact pedicle, stored safely, and later inset in contact with denuded bone around the whole defect.
pitfalls: Pedicle transected by sphenoidotomy or posterior septectomy before harvest
Flap too small for the defect
Incision too high (olfaction)
Inset upside down (mucosa against the defect)
Tearing the flap at the maxillary crest by elevating downward over the crossing fibres
Dividing a pedicle that obstructs the airway before about 6 months, while the flap may still depend on it

procedures.name: Transmaxillary exposure of the pterygopalatine fossa
indications: Tumours of the PPF (juvenile angiofibroma, schwannoma, perineural spread) and biopsy
Access to the pterygoid base for transpterygoid approaches (lateral recess, Meckel's cave, petrous apex)
IMAX ligation for refractory epistaxis
Vidian neurectomy
procedures.corridor: Transnasal: wide middle meatal antrostomy (or medial maxillectomy) plus removal of the posterior maxillary wall; medially through the SPF and palatine perpendicular plate. For large juvenile angiofibromas two surgeons work binostril (four hands) through a partial posterior septectomy for countertraction; the nasopharyngeal part, often the hardest margin, may be taken transorally with a curved adenoid bipolar, especially in young patients.

preop.check: Tumour extent on MRI/CT: foramina involved (rotundum, vidian, IOF, pterygomaxillary fissure), ITF extension.
preop.why: Sets how far lateral and posterior to go.

preop.check: Vascularity; consider angiography and embolisation.
preop.why: JNA and vascular tumours bleed from IMAX and ICA branches. Embolisation reduces but does not replace intraoperative control of the IMAX: embolised vessels recanalise.

preop.check: Which side for the nasoseptal flap if reconstruction is needed.
preop.why: Harvest opposite the PPF side or raise it first.

steps.do: Wide maxillary antrostomy back to the posterior wall; optionally raise a rescue or full nasoseptal flap first.
steps.think: Protect the pedicle before any SPA work.

steps.do: Raise the lateral wall flap to the crista ethmoidalis; control the SPA and posterior septal artery at the SPF.
steps.think: Proximal control before opening the fossa. For access behind the SPA (e.g. to the lateral recess) it can occasionally be retracted downward, but it usually has to be divided and ligated: traction avulses it.

steps.do: Remove the posterior maxillary wall with Kerrison or drill from medial (SPF) to lateral, preserving the periosteum.
steps.think: Periosteum intact keeps fat and vessels contained until you are ready. For IMAX ligation alone a posterior wall window is enough; for tumour, finish all bone removal before opening the periosteum — the fossa contents are under tension and herniate into the nose, and a torn IMAX in herniating fat is hard to control.

steps.do: Incise the periosteum widely; find the IMAX by its pulsation in the fat (it runs lateral to medial), tease it out with a blunt probe, place two clips laterally and one medially and divide between them; control its branches in the anterior vascular layer.
steps.think: Bipolar the exposed fat before handling it: it is threaded with small vessels that otherwise ooze throughout the case. Vascular before neural: clip or bipolar branches before retraction. Coagulate every branch you expose — unrecognised branches can go into spasm and bleed heavily after surgery.

steps.do: Retract the vascular layer and fat laterally to expose the neural layer: V2 and foramen rotundum superolaterally, the PPG, and the vidian nerve and canal inferomedially.
steps.think: V2 and the vidian canal frame the pterygoid base; the vidian canal points back to the ICA genu.

steps.do: Extend as needed: drill the pterygoid base (transpterygoid), follow the lateral pterygoid plate into the ITF, or resect tumour from foramina.
steps.think: Stop lateral dissection behind the ET until the ICA is identified; drill the vidian canal only on its inferomedial side.

procedures.endpoints: PPF opened with the IMAX controlled, V2 and vidian nerve identified and the intended target (tumour, pterygoid base, ITF) reached with neurovascular structures accounted for.
pitfalls: Blunt fat dissection before IMAX control
Confusing palatovaginal and vidian canals
Drilling superolateral to the vidian canal
Sacrificing the NSF pedicle unnecessarily

procedures.name: Endoscopic choanal atresia repair (cross-over flap technique)
indications: Bilateral choanal atresia in the neonate, once an oral airway is secured ([[dz.choanal-atresia]])
Unilateral choanal atresia with obstruction or discharge
procedures.corridor: Transnasal along the floor with a 0° endoscope alone (small-diameter in neonates) and fine, sometimes otologic-size, instruments; the new choana is made by removing the atretic plate and the posterior septum (vomer) and is lined with crossed mucosal flaps from the posterior septum and nasal floor of both sides.

preop.check: CT: plate composition, skull base height and the width of the posterior nasal cavity on both sides ([[v.choanal-atresia]]).
preop.why: Sets how low and how far medially to work; a low skull base above the plate forbids superior dissection.

preop.check: Septal deviation.
preop.why: It commonly coexists and narrows the corridor further; plan for it.

steps.do: Decongest topically (allow at least 5 minutes) and out-fracture the IT with a Freer to widen the posterior corridor.
steps.think: Room first: the whole operation is done along the floor with a 0° scope.

steps.do: Infiltrate saline under the posterior septal and nasal floor mucosa to lift it for the flaps.
steps.think: Hydrodissection makes thin mucosa easier to cut to shape and elevate.

steps.do: Incise the posterior septal mucosa about 1 cm in front of the atretic plate and carry the cut onto the nasal floor toward the IT tail — an L-shape on one side and its mirror J-shape on the other — and raise the flaps.
steps.think: Each flap must be long enough to cross to the other side of the new choana.

steps.do: Remove the posterior septum (vomer) and the atretic plate, taking the upper limit no higher than the lower edge of the MT; widen laterally as needed.
steps.think: Stay low and medial: the skull base lies just above the plate.

steps.do: Cross the flaps so that together they cover the whole raw neochoana, floor and roof; hold them with fibrin glue or a soft anchored pack for 1–2 days.
steps.think: No bare bone: covered bone is what prevents restenosis.

steps.do: Postoperative: saline irrigation at least three times daily for the first month (very small volumes in neonates), a short tapering course of topical steroid drops, no suction catheters in the first weeks, and endoscopy at about 10 days and then periodically through the first year.
steps.think: A blind suction catheter can displace the flaps.

procedures.endpoints: A widened choana on the affected side(s) with the atretic plate and posterior vomer removed below the level of the MT's lower edge, and all raw bone covered by mucosal flaps.
pitfalls: Dissecting above the lower edge of the MT (skull base)
Leaving raw bone uncovered (restenosis)
Ignoring a coexisting septal deviation that narrows the corridor
Late obstruction, years later, from hypertrophy of the posterior IT at the septal defect; partial turbinectomy helps selected patients

procedures.name: Balloon sinus dilation (balloon-only and hybrid)
indications: Recurrent acute or chronic rhinosinusitis without polyps limited to the maxillary, frontal or sphenoid outflow (focal, ostium-limited disease)
Selected patients in the office under local anaesthesia, avoiding a general anaesthetic
Hybrid use during conventional FESS, most often for the frontal outflow
procedures.corridor: Transnasal under endoscopic view: a guide catheter angled for each sinus, a (usually illuminated) guidewire through the outflow, and a balloon inflated over the wire. A balloon-only procedure removes no bone and cannot treat the ethmoid, whose many septated cells have no single dilatable ostium; a hybrid adds conventional instruments at any point of the dissection.

preop.check: Polyps or ethmoid disease on CT and endoscopy.
preop.why: Dilating an ostium does not clear polyps or ethmoid cells; these patients need conventional or hybrid surgery.

preop.check: Septal deviation, large IT, concha bullosa, tortuous or complex frontal outflow.
preop.why: Each can stop the catheter or balloon from reaching the ostium.

preop.check: Sphenoid: ICA and optic canal dehiscence ([[v.ica-dehiscence]], [[v.optic-canal-dehiscence]]).
preop.why: Sphenoid wire passage is essentially blind, so a dehiscent carotid or optic nerve is directly at risk.

preop.check: Frontal: outflow narrowed by osteitis or an osteoma.
preop.why: Inflating in a rigid, narrow tract can transmit force to the posterior table (fracture, CSF leak).

steps.do: Maxillary: place the angled catheter behind the uncinate pointing inferolaterally toward the natural ostium, pass the wire into the antrum and confirm it by transillumination of the cheek, then inflate a balloon whose diameter sets the size of the opening.
steps.think: The wire should advance with smooth, light pressure; resistance means a submucosal tract — withdraw and redirect.

steps.do: Frontal: use a catheter angled about 70°; spin the slightly bent wire tip to find the recess without moving the catheter; confirm the position by transillumination and, for a long recess, dilate serially from above downward.
steps.think: A sharp spot of light on the forehead that moves with the wire means frontal sinus; a diffuse glow means an ethmoid or suprabullar cell, the classic false passage. Taking the uncinate first can ease wire entry, but dilating before any dissection keeps the field dry.

steps.do: Sphenoid: pass the wire into the sphenoid ostium medial to the superior turbinate and dilate; confirm with fluoroscopy or navigation when unsure.
steps.think: There is no reliable transillumination check here: the wire passes blind toward the carotid and optic prominences.

steps.do: Hybrid: after dilation remove bony overhangs and mucosal tags bluntly or with a powered instrument, and complete any ethmoid surgery conventionally.
steps.think: Avoid circumferential mucosal injury at a dilated outflow: it heals as a stenosis.

procedures.endpoints: Each targeted outflow dilated with the wire proven to be in the intended sinus, no circumferential mucosal injury, and any ethmoid or polyp disease handled by conventional (hybrid) surgery. Oozing for 24–48 hours is expected; packing is rarely needed.
pitfalls: Dilating a suprabullar or ethmoid cell instead of the frontal sinus
Forcing the wire against resistance (submucosal tract)
Choosing balloon-only for polyps or ethmoid disease
Blind sphenoid wire passage with a dehiscent ICA or optic nerve
Dilating an osteitic or osteoma-narrowed frontal outflow (posterior table fracture)
Circumferential mucosal trauma when trimming after dilation (stenosis)

procedures.name: Endoscopic Denker approach (anterior medial maxillectomy)
indications: Benign or malignant tumours attached to the prelacrimal, anterior, inferior or lateral walls of the maxillary sinus
PPF and ITF lesions needing straight, wide access
Odontogenic lesions and refractory chronic rhinosinusitis of the anterolateral antrum — the traditional Caldwell-Luc indications
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, 0° endoscope: an endoscopic medial maxillectomy extended forward through the piriform aperture and the medial part of the anterior maxillary wall below the infraorbital nerve (the endonasal form of Denker's open operation, also called total endoscopic anterior medial maxillectomy). With the medial wall and a segment of the anterior wall gone, straight instruments reach every antral wall, the PPF and the ITF without a sublabial or transseptal incision, avoiding the oral contamination and oroantral fistula risk of a gingivobuccal incision. A lesser variant, the endoscopic anterior maxillotomy, drills only a window in the anterior wall below the infraorbital foramen through a subperiosteal pocket at the piriform rim.

preop.check: Tumour attachment and the shape of the anterior maxilla on CT and MRI.
preop.why: Confirms that lesser routes cannot reach it ([[pr.maxillary-access-ladder]]) and plans the bone cuts around the attachment.

preop.check: Infraorbital foramen and canal position.
preop.why: The anterior window must stay below the nerve.

preop.check: Counsel for nasolacrimal duct division, cheek swelling and numbness.
preop.why: The duct is divided, and the infraorbital and anterior superior alveolar nerves lie close to the cuts.

steps.do: Incise with a needle-tip cautery under a 0° scope along the junction of nasal floor and lateral wall, and along the lateral wall forward and down to just in front of the IT head over the piriform rim.
steps.think: These incisions serve both the medial maxillectomy and the subperiosteal pocket on the face of the maxilla.

steps.do: Elevate subperiosteally over the piriform aperture onto the anterior maxilla until the infraorbital nerve is seen at its foramen.
steps.think: Seeing the nerve is what makes the anterior cut safe.

steps.do: Complete an endoscopic medial maxillectomy ([[p.medial-maxillectomy]]), keeping the nasolacrimal duct until the end and then dividing it obliquely.
steps.think: A sharp oblique cut leaves a duct that can still drain.

steps.do: Cut the maxillotomy: a superior cut toward the level of the sinus roof but below the infraorbital foramen, an inferior cut at the junction of nasal floor and medial wall, and a posterior cut along the posterior wall, joined to the medial maxillectomy; remove the segment en bloc with the tumour's bony attachment.
steps.think: Keep the window below the nerve and take no more piriform rim than needed: losing the rim can let the ala collapse.

steps.do: Clear and drill the attachment site; extend into the PPF or ITF with straight instruments as needed.
steps.think: The straight corridor is the point of the approach: use it for four-handed work.

procedures.endpoints: Every antral wall and, if needed, the PPF and ITF reachable with straight instruments; tumour removed with its bony attachment; infraorbital and anterior superior alveolar nerves preserved; nasolacrimal duct cleanly divided.
pitfalls: Cutting above the infraorbital foramen
Taking too much piriform rim (alar collapse)
Cheek swelling and pain, and upper lip or tooth numbness, from the anterior dissection
Choosing it when a lesser rung of the access ladder would reach the lesion

procedures.name: Posterior pedicle inferior turbinate flap
indications: A limited skull base defect when the nasoseptal flap is unavailable (after a posterior septectomy or wide sphenoidotomies, or with pedicle loss): a long, narrow flap whose anterior reach is limited
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, 0° endoscope; the inferior turbinate mucoperiosteum pedicled on the inferior turbinate branch of the sphenopalatine artery (a terminal branch of the [[s.posterior-lateral-nasal-artery]]). Stored in a large maxillary antrostomy.

preop.check: Pedicle: inferior turbinate surgery or tumour, or sphenopalatine artery ligation.
preop.why: Any of these excludes the flap; the alternatives are the contralateral nasoseptal flap or a regional flap.

preop.check: Expected flap area against the defect.
preop.why: Harvey's cadaver flaps were 54.0 ± 4.9 mm long and 22.1 ± 3.7 mm wide in the distal third ([[m.itf-dimensions]]); the atlas table quotes about 2.4 cm² ([[m.itf-area]]), a figure those dimensions do not support. Reach is limited anteriorly.

steps.do: Create a large maxillary antrostomy for storing the flap.
steps.think: Raise the flap early, before the resection.

steps.do: Incise the superior border of the flap down to bone, from the junction of the vertical palatine bone and the posteromedial maxilla horizontally forward to the head of the inferior turbinate at the piriform aperture.
steps.think: The cut goes to bone or the flap will not lift cleanly.

steps.do: Dissect the mucosa off the turbinate bone in a subperiosteal plane, inferiorly and then up to the lateral side of the turbinate bone, preserving the pedicled blood supply.
steps.think: Stay subperiosteal: the vessels are in the periosteum.

steps.do: Continue superiorly to the apex of the inferior meatus; incise and free the mucosa there, away from the lacrimal duct. Further forward the freeing incision can lie more laterally to widen the flap.
steps.think: This makes a narrowing in the flap; the cut protects the duct.

steps.do: Place the flap and complete the multilayered reconstruction as for the posterior nasoseptal flap.
steps.think: Mucosa faces the nasal cavity; raw surface to cleaned bone.

procedures.endpoints: Flap covers the defect with its pedicle intact and no functional mucosa buried beneath it.
pitfalls: Using the flap for a defect larger than its small area
Entering the lacrimal duct at the apex of the inferior meatus
Raising it after prior inferior turbinate surgery or sphenopalatine ligation

procedures.name: Middle turbinate flap
indications: Small defects of the fovea ethmoidalis, planum sphenoidale or sella when the nasoseptal flap is not available: technically challenging, with very variable dimensions that depend on the turbinate
Midline defects from the transplanum to the transsellar region (atlas Table 31.2)
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, 0° endoscope; the middle turbinate mucosa raised from both its medial and lateral surfaces on the middle turbinate branch of the sphenopalatine artery.

steps.do: Make a vertical incision at the head of the middle turbinate.
steps.think: Check the turbinate's length first (> 4 cm for the sella).

steps.do: Make a horizontal incision at the superior medial aspect of the turbinate, below its attachment to the lateral lamella of the cribriform plate.
steps.think: Too high risks a CSF leak: stay below the cribriform plate.

steps.do: Elevate the medial and lateral mucosa from the bone in a subperiosteal plane with sharp instruments, then remove the turbinate bone piecemeal with through-cutting forceps.
steps.think: The bone is removed from inside the mucosal envelope.

steps.do: Incise the mucosa in the axilla to detach the lateral mucosa from the nasal wall, below the cribriform plate again, and continue inferiorly and posteriorly to free the lateral mucosa completely.
steps.think: The flap is then unfolded like a book.

steps.do: Dissect the pedicle back toward the sphenopalatine foramen for extra length.
steps.think: Length decides reach.

steps.do: Place the flap and complete the multilayered reconstruction as for the posterior nasoseptal flap.
steps.think: Mucosa toward the nasal cavity.

procedures.endpoints: Flap covers the defect with its pedicle intact.
pitfalls: A turbinate shorter than about 4 cm for a sellar defect
Cutting the superior incision too high (CSF leak)
Concha bullosa or hypoplasia not recognised on imaging

preop.check: Imaging of the middle turbinate: length, concha bullosa, hypoplasia.
preop.why: The turbinate must be longer than about 4 cm for the flap to reach the sella; a concha bullosa or hypoplastic turbinate makes the dissection harder.

preop.check: Pedicle: the internal maxillary artery (prior infratemporal fossa surgery or tumour).
preop.why: The atlas lists the middle turbinate flap among the flaps excluded when the internal maxillary artery is unavailable; prior sphenoid surgery and posterior septectomy endanger the septal branch, i.e. the nasoseptal flap.

procedures.name: Lateral nasal wall flap (anterior or posterior pedicle)
indications: Anterior pedicle (Hadad-Bassagaisteguy 2): reconstruction of anterior skull base defects in selected patients, after endonasal resection of an esthesioneuroblastoma or of a meningoencephalocele
Posterior pedicle (Carrau-Hadad): large median defects of the planum, sella, clivus and nasopharynx
procedures.corridor: Transnasal, 0° endoscope; the mucoperiosteum of the inferolateral nasal wall, based anteriorly or posteriorly.

steps.do: Raise the inferolateral nasal wall mucoperiosteum, with the anterior pedicle for anterior defects or the posterior pedicle for median ones.
steps.think: Choose the pedicle by where the defect is and which arteries are intact.

steps.do: Transpose to the defect, raw surface to bone.
steps.think: These are cadaver-derived techniques with a handful of clinical cases each.

procedures.endpoints: Flap covers the defect with its pedicle intact.
pitfalls: Choosing a flap whose pedicle was divided by an earlier approach

procedures.name: Septodermoplasty (Saunders) for HHT epistaxis
indications: Moderate to severe epistaxis in [[dz.hht]] that medical and office measures have not controlled. Telangiectasia recurs after every local treatment, so the operation buys time: in an audit of 301 procedures in 131 patients (33 septodermoplasties, 268 KTP laser treatments) 78.3% of patients needed three or fewer procedures, and the mean interval between treatments was 473 days (SD 515) (Harvey 2008).

Place in the sequence: in 50 patients mild-to-moderate disease did well with sequential argon laser with or without septodermoplasty or hormones, while severe disease (more than one transfusion) stopped bleeding only with closure of the nostrils, [[p.young-procedure]] (Lund 1999).

A septal perforation in a transfusion-dependent patient: septectomy combined with dermoplasty in 9 patients gave a lasting improvement in quality of life and lower transfusion requirements (22.61 to 9.57; the abstract does not give the unit), because a perforation makes graft take less likely (Lesnik 2007).
procedures.corridor: Transnasal over the septum. The one modern variant described in the sources read uses a caudal hemitransfixion incision, one side at a time (Burckhardt 2013).

preop.check: HHT diagnosis, how severe the bleeding is (transfusion and iron needs), and whether the septum is already perforated.
preop.why: Severity decides septodermoplasty against closure (Lund 1999). A perforation reduces the chance of a successful graft, which is why septectomy was combined with it (Lesnik 2007). Atraumatic technique and non-adherent packing apply as for any HHT nasal operation ([[dz.hht]]).

preop.check: Counsel on what the operation does and does not do.
preop.why: Recurrence of telangiectasia is inevitable and further laser is needed (Harvey 2008); smell is reduced and sinus infection more likely (Burckhardt 2013, describing the original operation).

steps.do: Make a caudal hemitransfixion incision and raise the septal mucosa off the perichondrium in a supra-perichondrial plane with a Cottle dissector, creating an upper and a lower tunnel on that side.
steps.think: Stay on the perichondrium: the graft needs it as its bed, and a hole through it is a perforation ([[h.septal-perforation]]). This step is described in a single case report (Burckhardt 2013); the abstracts of the larger series do not give the technique.

steps.do: Remove the telangiectatic septal mucosa. In the single case reported, small upper and lower mucosal flaps were left to cover the graft edges.
steps.think: The original operation eliminates the nasal mucosa and replaces it with a skin graft, usually from the thigh and sometimes from the oral mucosa (Saunders 1960, as described in Burckhardt 2013).

steps.do: Lay the graft on the perichondrium. In the classic operation it is skin; in the reported variant a synthetic dural graft was used instead, which avoids a distant donor site. Fix it with an absorbable transfixing suture and an absorbable hemostatic dressing.
steps.think: Graft take was 100% in a Japanese series of 15 patients (Ichimura 2006). The synthetic graft rests on one patient with a year of follow-up and no perforation (Burckhardt 2013).

steps.do: Treat the other side as a separate stage: the single case reported did the second side three months after the first.
steps.think: Whether both sides can be done in one stage is not stated in the sources read.

steps.do: Follow up for peripheral telangiectasia at the graft margins and treat it with laser as it appears.
steps.think: Septodermoplasty reduced the rate of subsequent KTP laser treatments from 1.83 to 0.78 (p = 0.012; Harvey 2008, units not defined in the abstract), so it lengthens the interval between treatments; it does not end them.

endpoints: Diseased septal mucosa replaced with a graft that has taken, on intact perichondrium
Fewer and shorter-interval bleeds, with laser available for margin telangiectasia
pitfalls: Promising a cure: telangiectasia recurs (Harvey 2008).
Grafting over an existing perforation without addressing it (Lesnik 2007).
Loss of smell and more sinus infections after the original operation (Burckhardt 2013).

In a systematic review of 20 studies (546 patients) the commonest complications of the surgeries studied were partial dehiscence of a nasal closure, septal perforation and continued bleeding needing reoperation (Benaim 2025); the abstract does not split the figures by operation.

procedures.name: Young's procedure (nasal closure) and its modifications
indications: Severe, transfusion-dependent epistaxis in [[dz.hht]] that other treatment has not controlled. In 50 patients, severe disease (more than one transfusion) did not benefit from laser but stopped bleeding after closure of the nostrils (Lund 1999).

A permanent operation for a carefully selected few: of 10 patients in a Danish cohort none was free of complications and one asked for reversal, and the authors reserve the procedure for selected patients (Andersen 2020).
procedures.corridor: The skin of the nasal vestibule at the mucocutaneous junction, usually both sides: closure prevents air passing through the nasal cavity (Lund 2017).

preop.check: Counselling about permanence and side effects, and a trial of functional closure.
preop.why: The commonest complaint was loss of smell and taste (Lund 2017). Obligate mouth breathing, dryness, worse sleep apnea and wound breakdown with revision are expected side effects, and a reported case of posterior bleeding after closure needed multiple transfusions, intubation, bilateral embolization and reversal, because the nostrils could no longer be used for access (Timmins 2016). Timmins recommends a trial of functional closure with petroleum-jelly-soaked cotton balls in the nostrils before the permanent operation.

preop.check: Laser photocoagulation of telangiectasias before closure.
preop.why: The procedure is usually combined with laser photocoagulation of the telangiectasias before closure (Timmins 2016).

steps.do: Make a circumferential incision through the skin at the mucocutaneous junction in the nasal vestibule.
steps.think: This is the two-flap method (Timmins 2016). The traditional closure is a three-flap modified Young's procedure (the current standard is a modification of the nasal closure first reported for HHT by Lund and Howard), which may be combined with a lateral alotomy for an additional internal flap closure (Timmins 2016). The sources read do not give the three-flap design.

steps.do: Elevate the skin back over the cartilage to make two flaps, far enough for a tension-free closure.
steps.think: Is the closure tension-free? Dehiscence is the failure mode.

steps.do: Close the two flaps to each other in a single layer (4-0 chromic suture in Timmins 2016), then repeat on the other side.
steps.think: Both sides were closed from the start (ab initio) in 81% of Lund's 100 patients (Lund 2017). In 13 patients 5 had the three-flap closure, all of whom needed revision for dehiscence, against 3 of 8 with the two-flap closure; operating time was 3.12 hours against 1.44 hours (p = 0.0001) with no difference in epistaxis score or benefit score (Timmins 2016) — a single-centre comparison of small, successive groups.

steps.do: Follow up for pinpoint openings and dehiscence along the line of closure and revise when bleeding resumes.
steps.think: Six of 13 patients developed pinpoint openings; four of the six had no increase in bleeding, so a small air leak can be managed expectantly (Timmins 2016). Partial dehiscence is the commonly reported complication and is usually treated with revision surgery (Bickerton 2025, scoping review of 192 patients).

endpoints: Both nostrils sealed with a tension-free closure and no airflow through the nasal cavity
pitfalls: Tension at the closure, and dehiscence (Timmins 2016; Bickerton 2025).
Weak selection or counselling: reversal requested by one of 10 in a Danish cohort (Andersen 2020), while none of 43 asked for reversal in a three-centre series (Richer 2012).

Overstating benefit. Complete cessation of bleeding was reported in 94% (Lund 2017, 100 patients; the denominator for that figure is not stated in the abstract, which says 50 completed the questionnaires) and in 30 of 36 patients (83%) with a mean hemoglobin rise of 4.68 g/dL after a mean of 34 months (Richer 2012, 43 patients). These are uncontrolled series of selected patients.
Posterior epistaxis after closure may be hard to control with the nostrils closed (Timmins 2016).

procedures.name: Transantral internal maxillary artery ligation
indications: Intractable posterior epistaxis after posterior nasal packing. Transantral ligation and percutaneous embolization were the two most common therapies in a 21-patient comparison (12 embolization, 5 ligation, 4 both) and had success rates of 89% and 94%, with no mortality or serious morbidity (Strong 1995). The authors conclude the choice should follow the individual patient.

Today endoscopic ligation of the terminal branches ([[p.spa-ligation]]) or transmaxillary IMAX control ([[p.ppf-exposure]]) is usually the first surgical choice; the transantral route remains where an endoscopic route is not available or has failed.
procedures.corridor: Caldwell-Luc (sublabial) antrostomy, then the posterior wall of the antrum to the pterygomaxillary fossa, where the artery is clipped (Morgan 1997).

preop.check: Age, anemia and hypertension; the possibility of bleeding from other sources.
preop.why: Advanced age, anemia and a history of hypertension predicted failure in 100 consecutive patients; of 15 who bled afterwards, causes found in 12 were failure to identify the artery in the pterygomaxillary space (6), blood flow through partly closed clips (2), posterior ethmoidal arteries (2) and revascularization of the nasal blood supply (2) (Metson 1988).

preop.check: Is an endoscopic or embolization route better for this patient?
preop.why: The reported success rates are comparable and each has its strengths and weaknesses (Strong 1995). Pritikin 1998 quotes average rates of 89% (transantral) and 94% (embolization) and complication rates of 28% and 27% from the literature; that is a secondary figure.

steps.do: Sublabial incision above the gingival sulcus, subperiosteal exposure of the anterior wall and a small antrostomy through the canine fossa ([[p.canine-fossa-trephination]]).
steps.think: The commonest complications are damage to the infraorbital nerve and the anterior superior alveolar nerve (Morgan 1997). In a comparison of 46 ligations with 30 controls, success and complication rates were both higher with ligation, and the authors call it valid only if infraorbital nerve injury is avoided (McDonald 1980).

steps.do: Through the antrum, remove a window in the posterior wall, incise the periosteum and find the internal maxillary artery in the pterygomaxillary fossa; the layers are described in [[p.ppf-exposure]].
steps.think: Have I found the artery? Failure to identify it in the pterygomaxillary space was the commonest cause of surgical failure in Metson 1988. The third segment branches variably in the fossa, which can leave a branch uncontrolled (Morton 1991, cadaver series). The abstracts do not describe the posterior wall step itself; it is standard in the operation and is not sourced here.

steps.do: Clip the artery. Only the trunk need be ligated (Nair 1982); check that every clip closes the vessel completely.
steps.think: Blood flow through partly closed clips caused two of the failures in Metson 1988.

steps.do: Fashion a nasoantral window if the natural ostium is not intact, then close the sublabial wound.
steps.think: A nasoantral window is optional and depends on the integrity of the sinus ostium; the oroantral fistulas reported after the operation were in patients with no window (Morgan 1997, two cases).

steps.do: If bleeding recurs, look for the causes found in Metson 1988: an unclipped artery or branch, a leaking clip, posterior ethmoidal arteries ([[p.aea-ligation]]) or collateral supply; embolization is the other route (Strong 1995).
steps.think: Re-explore or image before repeating a clip: in Metson 1988 re-exploration or angiography established the cause in 12 of the 15 failures.

endpoints: Internal maxillary artery clipped and bleeding controlled
Sublabial wound closed, with drainage of the antrum assured
pitfalls: Failing to find the artery (Metson 1988).
Partly closed clips (Metson 1988).
Infraorbital or anterior superior alveolar nerve injury (McDonald 1980; Morgan 1997).
Oroantral fistula where no nasoantral window was made (Morgan 1997).
Over-reading the success rates: they come from small retrospective series of intractable bleeding with selection effects, and the comparison in Strong 1995 has 21 patients.

stations.name: Nasal cavity and lateral wall overview
stations.where: Overview camera lateral to the face, looking medially at a sagittal cut through the nasal cavity just lateral to the septum.
stations.purpose: Orientation: turbinates, meati and the nasopharynx in one view before any endoscopic station.

stations.name: First pass: floor to nasopharynx
stations.where: Scope tip advanced along the nasal floor medial to the inferior turbinate to the choana, looking posteriorly.
stations.purpose: First pass of diagnostic endoscopy: septum, IT, choana and nasopharynx including both fossae of Rosenmüller.

stations.name: Nasopharynx: Eustachian tube and fossa of Rosenmüller
stations.where: Scope tip at the choana, angled lens rotated laterally toward the lateral nasopharyngeal wall.
stations.purpose: Inspect the fossa of Rosenmüller behind the torus, the commonest site of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

stations.name: Second pass: sphenoethmoidal recess
stations.where: Scope tip between the middle turbinate and septum, advanced to the posterior nasal cavity, looking posteriorly and superiorly.
stations.purpose: Second pass: superior turbinate, sphenoid ostium and SER drainage; the sphenoid ostium lies medial to the superior turbinate about 1–1.5 cm above the choana.

stations.name: Third pass: middle meatus
stations.where: Scope tip at the head of the middle turbinate, entering the middle meatus under it, looking laterally.
stations.purpose: Third pass and the start of every FESS: uncinate, hiatus semilunaris, bulla, accessory ostia.

stations.name: Infundibulum and maxillary natural ostium
stations.where: Scope tip in the anterior middle meatus after uncinectomy, lens rotated laterally into the infundibulum.
stations.purpose: Confirm the natural ostium before enlarging; see the orbit as the lateral wall of the infundibulum.

stations.name: Maxillary antrum through the antrostomy
stations.where: Scope tip at the middle meatal antrostomy, lens turned anterolaterally into the maxillary sinus.
stations.purpose: Inspect recesses the 0° cannot see; locate the infraorbital nerve before instrumenting the roof.

stations.name: Inferior meatus and valve of Hasner
stations.where: Scope tip under the anterior inferior turbinate (IT gently medialised), lens rotated superolaterally.
stations.purpose: Find the nasolacrimal opening before inferior meatal work or IT surgery; check DCR/NLD patency.

stations.name: Anterior septum and nasal valve
stations.where: Scope tip just inside the vestibule, directed medially and posteriorly along the septum.
stations.purpose: Epistaxis source (Kiesselbach area), valve narrowing and anterior deviations before septoplasty.

stations.name: Lateral wall at the MT axilla (DCR)
stations.where: Scope tip in the anterior nasal cavity, facing the lateral wall at the middle turbinate axilla.
stations.purpose: Plan the DCR mucosal flap and bone window; the sac extends 8–10 mm above the axilla.

stations.name: Sphenopalatine foramen and crista ethmoidalis
stations.where: Scope tip in the posterior middle meatus under the MT tail, looking laterally at the lateral wall after the mucoperiosteal flap is raised.
stations.purpose: SPA ligation: every branch behind the crista, including the posterior septal branch.

stations.name: Sphenoid face and nasoseptal flap pedicle
stations.where: Scope tip in the posterior nasal cavity at the level of the superior turbinate, looking posteriorly at the anterior sphenoid face and choana.
stations.purpose: Plan flap incisions and protect the pedicle between the sphenoid ostium and the choanal arch.

stations.name: PPF through the posterior maxillary wall
stations.where: Scope tip in a wide middle meatal antrostomy (or medial maxillectomy), looking posteriorly after removal of the posterior maxillary wall and periosteum.
stations.purpose: The anterior vascular layer and the posterior neural layer of the PPF; V2 and vidian canal frame the pterygoid base.

stations.name: PPF and ITF overview
stations.where: Overview camera anterolateral to the face with the maxilla and zygoma rendered transparent, looking posteromedially.
stations.purpose: How the PPF opens into the ITF, and the ITF landmarks (plate to V3, ET to ICA).

pathways.name: Maxillary mucociliary clearance
pathways.note: Star-shaped from the floor up all walls to the natural ostium, then through the infundibulum and hiatus into the middle meatus, and back over the IT to pass in front of and below the Eustachian tube orifice.

pathways.name: Mucus recirculation through a separate opening
pathways.note: Pathological loop: mucus leaves by the natural ostium and re-enters through an accessory ostium or an antrostomy that was not joined to it. Joining the openings breaks the loop.

pathways.name: Posterior sinus clearance to the nasopharynx
pathways.note: Posterior ethmoid and sphenoid secretions pass through the superior meatus and SER and cross above and behind the torus tubarius, unlike the anterior group, which passes below the ET orifice: postnasal drip above the torus points to the posterior sinuses.

pathways.name: Lacrimal drainage
pathways.note: Tears pass from the puncta through the canaliculi and common canaliculus into the sac, down the NLD and out under the IT. A DCR bypasses the NLD by opening the sac into the middle meatus.
